findings.title: Default token-signing secret permits forging any user session
findings.description: When TOKEN_SECRET is unset, authentication tokens are signed with the public literal `workspace-dev-secret`. An unauthenticated caller can reproduce the HMAC format in src/lib/tokens.ts and mint a valid bearer token for any known user ID, including usr_root; authenticate then trusts the user ID returned by readToken and loads the corresponding user. This bypasses login and grants admin privileges.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-supplied organization ID without membership validation
findings.description: Billing routes are mounted before resolveOrg in app.ts, so the organization membership check is never applied to them. billing.ts selects organization using arbitrary X-Org-Id for plan and invoices endpoints. Any authenticated manager (role allowed by securityRules for /api/billing) can request another tenant's billing plan and invoice data by supplying its org ID.

findings.title: Cross-organization invoice PDF disclosure
findings.description: Any authenticated user can request an invoice PDF by ID. The route calls pdfService.render(req.params.id), which looks up the invoice without checking the caller's organization and includes the invoice's internalNote in the returned document. A user who learns or guesses another organization's invoice ID can read its customer, line items, and internal note.

findings.title: Task move permits cross-organization project reassignment
findings.description: taskService.move authorizes the source task through the caller's organization, but fetches the destination project globally and never verifies target.orgId equals user.orgId. A member who owns a task can move it into another organization's project, changing task orgId to the victim org and potentially exposing or corrupting data there.

Unlike the global resolveOrg middleware, which rejects a non-admin request selecting another org, billing is mounted before resolveOrg and orgOf() never applies that membership check. A manager in one organization can retrieve another organization's plan/payment suffix and invoice summaries by supplying its org ID.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint bypasses organization ownership check
findings.description: The invoice PDF route passes the requested ID directly to pdfService.render. That service loads the invoice globally by ID and does not compare invoice.orgId with the authenticated user's organization. Other invoice routes use invoiceService.get(user,id), which performs organization scoping. An authenticated user who obtains or guesses another tenant's invoice ID can retrieve its customer, line items, totals, and internal note.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint exposes cross-organization invoice data
findings.description: Any authenticated API user can request GET /api/invoices/:id/pdf for an invoice ID in another organization. The route calls pdfService.render(id), which loads the invoice by ID without a user/org argument or tenant check, and returns customer, line items, total, and internalNote. Other invoice routes use invoiceService.get(user,id), which enforces org ownership; this PDF route bypasses it.

findings.title: Non-production startup seeds a known platform-admin credential
findings.description: Whenever NODE_ENV is anything other than exactly production (including unset), server startup seeds usr_root as a platform admin with the fixed passcode pw-root. The public login endpoint accepts that passcode and issues a valid bearer token. If a non-production deployment is reachable by untrusted users, an attacker can log in as the platform admin and access admin functionality. Runtime exposure is unverified.

findings.title: Predictable default service token exposes internal API
findings.description: When SERVICE_TOKEN is unset, internal routes accept the fixed literal svc-dev-token. The token gates /api/internal/invoices/:id, exports, and Slack comment integration; an unauthenticated caller who knows the source default can retrieve any invoice by ID, export any project, or submit comments as a same-organization author. This requires deployment without SERVICE_TOKEN configured.

findings.title: Predictable default signing secret permits forged bearer tokens
findings.description: When TOKEN_SECRET is unset, all tokens use the literal workspace-dev-secret. Anyone who can reach the deployed API and knows this source can mint a valid HMAC token for any existing user ID, then access authenticated endpoints as that account. Exploitation depends on deployment leaving TOKEN_SECRET unset; token verification itself correctly checks the HMAC.

findings.title: Public board export discloses private project tasks
findings.description: An unauthenticated caller can request GET /public/boards/:slug/export for a published board. The route obtains the published board and calls exportService.exportProject(board.projectId); exportProject serializes every task returned by listForProject without filtering visibility, including private task titles and notes. The companion publicView explicitly filters visibility === "public", demonstrating that the export bypasses that restriction. Seed data includes a private task with confidential notes.

findings.title: Public board export discloses private project tasks and notes
findings.description: The unauthenticated /public/boards/:slug/export handler verifies only that the board is published, then passes its projectId to exportService.exportProject. That service returns every task's title, notes, status and visibility, without filtering to public tasks. By contrast, publicView explicitly filters tasks to visibility === "public". Anyone who knows a published board slug can therefore retrieve private task content and notes for its project.

findings.title: Task history endpoint returns activity across organizations
findings.description: GET /api/tasks/:id/history does not call taskService.require or any equivalent tenant check. It calls activityService.forEntity("task", req.params.id), and the service queries activity solely by entity and entityId, without orgId. An authenticated user who knows or guesses a task ID can retrieve its history, including actor IDs and details.

findings.title: Task move permits moving tasks into another organization
findings.description: An authenticated user who can write a task can submit POST /api/tasks/:id/move with another organization's projectId. taskService.move checks the source task's org through requireWritable, but fetches the target project by ID without checking target.orgId against user.orgId, then updates both projectId and orgId. This transfers the task and its data to the foreign organization.

findings.title: Authentication registration accepts empty passcodes
findings.description: The public registration handler forwards arbitrary body data to authService.register, where passcode is coerced to a string and hashed without a minimum-strength or non-empty check. This permits creating an account with an empty passcode; login accepts the same empty passcode, making such accounts trivially accessible to anyone who knows the email. This is self-selected during signup rather than takeover of existing accounts, so impact is limited to newly registered accounts.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-controlled organization header
findings.description: The billing router derives the target organization directly from X-Org-Id when present, then uses that ID to return plan details (including payment method last four), invoices, and usage. These routes are mounted behind general API authentication and securityRules, whose billing rule permits manager/admin roles, but no check binds the supplied organization ID to the authenticated user's organization. Any authenticated manager can therefore read another organization's billing metadata and invoice summaries by supplying its ID.

findings.title: Search leaks comments across organization boundaries
findings.description: The authenticated search endpoint scopes task and project searches to user.orgId but commentRepo.search searches all comments globally, and searchService returns comment body snippets and task IDs without checking comment/task organization. A user can search distinctive text to discover and read snippets from other organizations.

findings.title: Invoice share tokens disclose full invoice details to unauthenticated callers
findings.description: The public invoice route accepts a valid, unexpired signed share token, but tokens can be issued for only one day by a manager and are bearer credentials. Any recipient can call the route without authentication; publicView returns customer, amount, status, and line descriptions. The token is properly MAC-verified and expiry checked, so this is intended share functionality rather than a token-forgery flaw; no issue unless the sharing policy expects more restricted fields.

findings.title: Default token signing secret enables forged bearer and share tokens
findings.description: When TOKEN_SECRET is unset, the application signs tokens with the public literal `workspace-dev-secret`. Since `readToken` uses the same value to validate bearer tokens, an unauthenticated caller who knows a user ID can compute a valid token and authenticate as that user. The same signing key also permits forging invoice share claims for known invoice IDs, bypassing the intended issuance authorization and expiry policy by choosing an expiry. The app config does not fail closed on the fallback.

findings.title: Attachment filename traversal enables writes outside upload root
findings.description: Authenticated users can upload an attachment whose filename contains path separators and dot segments. cleanName removes markup but preserves slash and dot characters, and storage.put joins the resulting value under uploadRoot without containment validation. Sufficient ../ segments in filename escape the upload directory and write attacker-controlled content to any filesystem path writable by the service account; the stored key can also later be read during download.

findings.title: Webhook delivery endpoint exposes stored authorization headers
findings.description: An authenticated user in an organization can GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. The service checks only that the webhook belongs to the user's org, then returns full delivery records including requestHeaders. Those headers contain the webhook Bearer authToken (also shown in seeded deliveries), disclosing a reusable credential to any org member.

findings.title: API key reads expose keys across an organization
findings.description: Any authenticated caller in an organization can list every API key or fetch any key by ID, regardless of ownership. apiKeyService.list filters only by orgId; require checks only orgId, and the route returns the complete row. This exposes key metadata to ordinary members; if key scope/label or associated credentials are treated as secrets, the code model contains no secret value itself, so impact is limited to cross-user API key inventory. Org admins can explicitly select another org through resolveOrg; key reads still require matching org, thereby granting cross-org reads to admins by design. Flag as medium because members can enumerate another member's key objects, but model has no key secret.

findings.title: Billing routes trust caller-supplied organization ID
findings.description: An authenticated manager/admin can choose an arbitrary organization using X-Org-Id on /api/billing/plan and /api/billing/invoices. The billing router is mounted before resolveOrg in src/app.ts, and its orgOf helper directly prefers the header. resolveOrg therefore never constrains these requests. The handlers pass that value to billingService, which returns target-organization plan/payment metadata and invoice summaries. A caller can read data from organizations they do not belong to.

findings.title: Billing routes trust X-Org-Id before organization authorization
findings.description: The /api/billing router is mounted before resolveOrg in createApp (src/app.ts:27-28), so requests to billing handlers do not pass through resolveOrg. billing.ts independently chooses the organization from the caller-controlled X-Org-Id header (lines 8-9), and uses it for plan and invoice lookups (lines 11-17). The global securityRules only requires manager/admin for the billing prefix; it does not establish membership in the requested organization. A signed-in manager can therefore set X-Org-Id to another organization's ID and read its plan and invoices. This is broken tenant authorization; exact data exposure depends on billingService/repository contents.

findings.title: Goal update permits cross-tenant field reassignment
findings.description: PUT /api/goals/:id is authenticated and goalService.update checks the existing goal's orgId before updating, but parseGoalInput accepts fields only name and target. This appears correctly scoped; no exploitable flaw identified.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint bypasses tenant authorization and exposes internal invoice notes
findings.description: Any authenticated API user who can obtain or guess another tenant's invoice ID can request GET /api/invoices/:id/pdf. Unlike adjacent invoice handlers, this route calls pdfService.render directly; render fetches by ID only and returns invoice number, customer, line items, totals, and internalNote. It never checks invoice.orgId against the authenticated user's organization. Tenant boundary is otherwise enforced by invoiceService.get. An attacker can therefore read another organization's invoice contents and internal notes.

findings.title: Label PUT permits overwriting immutable ownership and tenant fields
findings.description: An authenticated user can PUT /api/labels/:id for a label they own (or any label if role is not member). parseLabelInput returns only name/color, but labelService.update passes that input to a generic table.update. Inspecting the actual flow shows no mass-assignment of orgId/ownerId through this route, so this is not a valid finding.

findings.title: Public board export exposes private project task data
findings.description: Unauthenticated GET /public/boards/:slug/export requires only that the board is published, then passes its projectId to exportProject. That service is explicitly a full export and returns every project task's id, title, notes, status, and visibility without filtering visibility or checking caller authorization. A public slug for a published board therefore exposes private task notes and identifiers.

findings.title: Published board export exposes private project tasks
findings.description: An unauthenticated caller can request `/public/boards/:slug/export` for any published board. The route passes its projectId to exportProject, which serializes every project task including private task titles and notes, without applying the public-visibility filter used by publicView. This leaks private project data to anyone who knows a published board slug.

findings.title: Search leaks comments across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated user searching for any comment text receives matches from the global comments table, including each comment's body and taskId. Unlike task and project searches, commentRepo.search has no organization constraint, and searchService does not resolve each comment's task or check its org. Any member able to call GET /search?q=... can retrieve matching comments belonging to other organizations; the query can be iterated over likely terms to expose content.

findings.title: Service-token endpoint exports any project without project authorization
findings.description: A caller with the shared service token can request GET /api/internal/exports/:projectId for any project ID. The router only applies requireServiceToken; exportProject fetches that project directly and returns its task titles, notes, statuses, and visibility without checking tenant or caller access. A compromised or over-broad service-token holder can therefore retrieve project data across organizations.

findings.title: Task move accepts a destination project from another organization
findings.description: An authenticated user can move a task they can write into a project belonging to another organization. taskService.move first requires the task to belong to the caller's organization, but looks up the destination with projectRepo.get(projectId) and only checks that it exists; it then updates both projectId and orgId to the destination project's values. The repository's unscoped get/update operations allow this cross-tenant reassignment. This enables integrity tampering and can place task data in another tenant.

findings.title: Webhook delivery history exposes delivery credentials
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can call GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. webhookService verifies the webhook belongs to the user's org but returns delivery records verbatim, including requestHeaders. The seeded delivery records explicitly store Authorization: Bearer <webhook auth token>; callers with only the member role can therefore retrieve reusable webhook credentials for their organization.

findings.title: Webhook delivery listing exposes stored authorization headers
findings.description: WebhookDelivery models persist the full requestHeaders and requestBody. The authenticated GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries path calls webhookService.deliveries, which returns deliveriesFor(hook.id) unchanged; the route is before the manager-role middleware, and require() only checks matching orgId. A member in the webhook's organization can therefore read recorded outbound Authorization headers and obtain the webhook's bearer credential (and request payloads).

findings.title: Approval owners can self-approve requests by setting state
findings.description: Any authenticated member can create an approval with an arbitrary state, and can later update their own approval's state because canWrite permits the owner. The validator accepts any string as state and there is no transition/approver-role check. A member can POST /api/approvals with {subject:"...", state:"approved"}, or PUT their own approval with state changed to approved, causing the record to represent approval without an authorized approver.

findings.title: Approval state can be modified by any authenticated organization member
findings.description: PUT /api/approvals/:id verifies organization membership in the route param handler, but write authorization is only applied to the current owner or non-member roles. This appears correct. However approval input accepts arbitrary state strings; no transition constraints evident, but absent business rules cannot establish vulnerability.

findings.title: Expired invoice share tokens remain valid
findings.description: GET /public/invoices/:token checks the signed claim kind but never checks expiresAt against current time. readShareToken verifies HMAC integrity and parses expiry, but accepts expired claims; publicView then retrieves the invoice and returns customer, amount, status, and line details. Any previously issued invoice share token remains usable indefinitely after its stated expiry.

findings.title: Members can create and read or modify other owners' epics
findings.description: Any authenticated org member can create an epic, and the list/require methods expose all epics in the organization. The route exposes these operations without an org-role gate. In contrast, update/delete enforce ownership for members. If epics are intended to be manager-only, members can create records contrary to that policy; if per-owner confidentiality is intended, list and require disclose other owners' records. Existing code establishes org-level access rather than owner-level read confidentiality, so primary confirmed defect is missing manager check on create, allowing privilege bypass of intended manager-only creation evidenced by sibling sprint/tag services.

findings.title: Notes list discloses every note in organization
findings.description: An authenticated member can GET /api/notes and receive noteRepo.listForOrg(user.orgId), which returns every note in the organization without filtering ownerId. Other member-only note operations explicitly require ownership, showing cross-user read access exceeds the intended boundary. This exposes titles and bodies of coworkers’ notes.

findings.title: Notification list exposes all organization notifications
findings.description: An authenticated member can GET /api/notifications and receives all notification records for the active organization without owner filtering. Notifications may contain titles and channel values belonging to other members. Single-record mutation routes enforce ownership for members, but the list route does not.

findings.title: Organization members can read every member's reminders
findings.description: Any authenticated user in the active organization who knows a reminder ID can retrieve its full row, including message, remindAt and ownerId. The parameter loader checks only organization membership at lines 12–16, and GET returns the row without calling canWrite. PUT/DELETE explicitly restrict members to their own rows at lines 32–39, demonstrating owner-specific confidentiality/action policy elsewhere in the same router.

findings.title: Project task listing and export ignore private task visibility
findings.description: An authenticated user in a project's organization can call GET /api/projects/:id/tasks or GET /api/projects/:id/export. projectService.require checks only that the project belongs to the user's org; taskService.listForProject then returns every top-level task, and exportService serializes every task's notes/status/visibility without filtering. Tasks are created with visibility: "private" (taskService.ts:38), so users who are not authorized to view private tasks can retrieve those tasks and notes via these project endpoints. No per-task visibility check is present in either path.

findings.title: Reminder reads bypass owner authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated user in the same organization can GET a reminder by ID, regardless of ownerId. The param handler checks only that the row exists and belongs to req.org, then GET returns the row without calling canWrite or another owner check. This can expose another member's reminder message and scheduled time.

findings.title: Task history endpoint exposes activity across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated caller can request GET /api/tasks/:id/history using another organization's task ID. Unlike the other task subroutes, this handler does not call taskService.require or otherwise verify the task's organization; activityService.forEntity queries globally by entity and entityId and returns matching records. This exposes activity details and actor IDs across tenant boundaries when the task ID is known.

findings.title: Template list exposes every organization member's templates
findings.description: An authenticated member can list all templates in their organization, including templates owned by other users. The ID-based get checks organization membership, but listForOrg filters only by orgId and no owner/role policy narrows results. This exposes names and template bodies to any same-org member.

The :id parameter loader limits rows to the resolved org, but does not impose owner authorization. Trigger by issuing one of these methods against another owner's custom-field ID. This appears inconsistent with the intended owner check encoded in the other branch.

findings.title: Members can self-approve their own approval records

The approval routes are not restricted by securityRules; create stores the caller as owner, and canWrite permits the owner. ApprovalInput accepts caller-selected state. If state represents an approval decision, this lets requesters approve their own requests and bypass separation of duties.

findings.title: Project task listing and export expose private tasks to every organization member
findings.description: Any authenticated user in the project's organization can call GET /api/projects/:id/tasks or GET /api/projects/:id/export. Project authorization checks only orgId; taskService.listForProject returns every task for that project, and exportService also serializes every task including notes and visibility. Neither path filters private tasks or checks task ownership. A member who can identify a project can therefore read private task content belonging to other users.

findings.title: Task comment creation allows authorId spoofing

Because the request body is spread after authorId, a caller can supply another user's authorId; commentService.add persists the value directly. The final taskId and orgId cannot be overridden due to their later placement, but the author identity can be forged.

findings.title: Task comment endpoint allows author impersonation
findings.description: POST /tasks/:id/comments first verifies access to the task, but then constructs the comment with `{ authorId: user.id, ...req.body, taskId: task.id, orgId: task.orgId }`. Since the request body is spread after authorId, a caller can submit another authorId. commentService.add persists that value directly, enabling forged attribution in comments.

findings.title: Nested admin mutation routes bypass admin role enforcement
findings.description: SecurityConfig restricts only the single-segment pattern /api/admin/* to ROLE_ADMIN. Admin mutation routes are nested (for example /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and /api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits), so they fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). AdminService performs tenant checks but does not require an administrator role, and changeRole accepts any Role including ADMIN. Any authenticated tenant user can promote themselves (or another same-tenant user) to ADMIN and change tenant limits.

This bypasses tenant boundary and can misattribute/move financial records across tenants.

findings.title: Authenticated users can download other users’ receipts
findings.description: Receipt downloads do not bind the receipt to the authenticated caller or require authentication in the controller method. The global chain requires authentication for non-public routes, but any authenticated user who knows or obtains a receipt ID can download its bytes, even when it belongs to another tenant/expense. Other receipt operations check access through ExpenseService; download calls only load(receiptId).

findings.title: Billing endpoints allow cross-tenant invoice and plan reads
findings.description: Any authenticated user can choose an arbitrary X-Tenant-Id for the billing endpoints. A user from one tenant can retrieve another tenant's subscription and invoice records by changing the header.

findings.title: Billing routes bypass tenant context and lack enforced service authorization
findings.description: TenantFilter explicitly skips every URI beginning /api/billing. SecurityConfig requires authentication for ordinary routes but does not require SERVICE for /api/billing; the billing controller/service must therefore supply any needed role or tenant checks. BillingService operations that accept caller context without tenant scoping can cross tenant boundaries if exposed to ordinary authenticated users.

findings.title: Expense project reassignment bypasses tenant boundary
findings.description: Expense creation/update validates the referenced project belongs to the caller's tenant, but a project can later be reassigned through ProjectService and ExpenseRepository.reassign updates expense.projectId without checking each expense tenant/owner or destination project tenant. If a caller can reach the project transfer operation, expenses tied to a source project can be attached to an arbitrary destination project, potentially crossing tenant boundaries and exposing expense associations to the destination tenant. Verify transfer authorization path before treating this conditional chain as reachable.

findings.title: Export names allow path traversal outside export directory
findings.description: ExportService sanitizes the requested output name with Text.plain(), which only removes markup and normalizes whitespace, then resolves that value directly against exportDir before writing. A name containing ../ segments escapes the configured export directory and can overwrite/create CSV files at writable paths accessible to the service account.

findings.title: Global search exposes comments across tenants and ownership boundaries
findings.description:
CWE: CWE-639

The search endpoint is authenticated but comment search is global. Unlike expense search in the same method, which filters by tenant and owner/manager, comment results are neither constrained by user tenant nor by permissions on the associated expense. This permits cross-tenant or same-tenant peer disclosure if a user can guess/search comment content.

findings.title: Nested admin endpoints bypass ADMIN role restriction
findings.description: SecurityConfig restricts only /api/admin/* to ADMIN. In Spring path matching, * matches one path segment and does not cover nested routes such as /api/admin/users, /api/admin/tenants, or /api/admin/stats. Those routes fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). Controllers expose user listings and role changes/tenant limits without method-level admin checks. A same-tenant authenticated non-admin can therefore change user roles, including promoting themselves.

findings.title: Public statement share endpoint accepts valid tokens for any statement
findings.description: The public statement route validates that the supplied signed token is a statement share token, but ignores the token subject and builds the statement named by the independent path id. A valid share token for one statement therefore authorizes retrieval of any other statement when its ID is known.

findings.title: Vendor bank details endpoint lacks tenant manager authorization
findings.description: Unlike every neighboring vendor endpoint, PUT /api/tenants/{tenantId}/vendors/{id}/bank-details has no @PreAuthorize check. The service trusts the caller-supplied tenantId to locate the vendor and performs the bank account replacement. Any authenticated user can therefore modify bank details for a vendor in their own tenant, including a non-manager; tenant path cannot be changed to another tenant because findInTenant scopes lookup.

findings.title: Currency conversion can overflow before division

The service multiplies amountCents by source.rateMicros() as a signed long before division. For sufficiently large values the intermediate wraps, returning a mathematically incorrect converted amount; this can corrupt downstream financial calculations if consumers rely on the result.

findings.title: Department headcount accepts unbounded negative values
findings.description: A manager/admin can create or update a department with an arbitrary headcount, including negative values. The DTO integer is copied directly into the stored record without a range check; this permits corrupt department data and can undermine downstream reporting or capacity calculations.

findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver ID

findings.title: Cross-tenant expense transfer via foreign target project

findings.title: Export names permit path traversal and overwrite arbitrary files

findings.title: Global search exposes comments across tenants
findings.description: An authenticated user can request `/api/search?q=<at-least-3-character-query>` and receive matching comments from every tenant. `GlobalSearchService.search` scopes expenses by tenant and vendors by tenant, but calls `comments.search(q)` without a tenant/user constraint and returns each comment body in `SearchHit.title`. `CommentRepository.search` scans all stored comments. This bypasses tenant isolation and can disclose private comment contents and identifiers.

findings.title: Integration comment relay accepts caller-supplied tenant, expense and author
findings.description: A SERVICE-role caller can POST arbitrary CommentInput fields to /api/integrations/comments. The relay passes the object directly to CommentService.add, which persists its tenantId, expenseId and authorId without checking the expense exists or that the integration is authorized for that tenant. The public comment listing filters only by expenseId after verifying the caller can access that expense, so a fabricated comment placed under an existing expense becomes visible to its authorized readers; untrusted IDs also allow forged attribution.

findings.title: Integration comment relay trusts caller-supplied tenant and author
findings.description: The service-role-protected POST /api/integrations/comments endpoint passes the request body directly to CommentService.add. add stores tenantId, expenseId, and authorId from CommentInput without validating that the referenced expense exists or that the author belongs to the tenant. A caller holding a service credential can create comments attached to arbitrary expense IDs and spoof any author; comments for a real expense then appear in that expense's list to authorized viewers.

findings.title: Nested admin mutation routes bypass the admin role matcher
findings.description: SecurityConfig protects only `/api/admin/*`, which matches a single segment below `/api/admin`. The controller exposes deeper mutation paths `/api/admin/users/{id}/roles`, `/api/admin/users/{id}/deactivate`, and `/api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits`; these do not match the admin-only rule and fall through to `anyRequest().authenticated()`. Consequently any authenticated user can invoke role changes, deactivate users, or update their own tenant limits. The service enforces tenant equality but does not require an administrator role; role authorization is solely the route matcher.

findings.title: Project expense listing bypasses expense ownership checks
findings.description: A tenant user can request GET /api/projects/{id}/expenses for a project in their tenant. ProjectService.expensesOf checks only that the project belongs to the caller's tenant, then queries all expenses assigned to that project and returns their fields without applying ExpenseService.get's owner-or-manager authorization or ExpenseService.list's owner filter. This exposes other employees' expense descriptions, amounts, vendors, dates and status to any same-tenant user able to identify a project with expenses.

findings.title: Public share endpoint does not bind token to requested statement
findings.description: POST /api/statements/{id}/share is ownership-checked before issuing a token for that id. However, the directly related public statement reader validates only that the supplied token has a signed `stmt:` subject, then independently loads the path id; it never compares token subject to path id. A valid share token for any statement therefore authorizes retrieval of any other statement when paired with its id. This scope was specifically the StatementController routes; the flaw in the consumer is described as a consequence of this controller's share token issuance and appears in PublicStatementController.

findings.title: Public statement share tokens are not bound to requested statement
findings.description: The public statement endpoint verifies that a supplied token is a valid statement share token but discards its subject, then returns the statement selected by the caller-controlled path ID. Any valid share token can therefore be paired with another known statement ID to disclose that statement.

findings.title: Receipt downloads lack expense/tenant authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated caller can download a receipt by its receiptId without checking access to the associated expense or tenant. ReceiptController.download calls receipts.load(receiptId), and ReceiptService.load performs only a repository lookup. Receipt IDs are generated from a process-wide incrementing counter (Ids.next), making neighboring identifiers predictable; an authenticated user who learns one receipt ID can try adjacent IDs and retrieve other users' receipt contents.

findings.title: CSV export leaves spreadsheet formulas executable
findings.description: Expense descriptions are inserted into downloadable CSV fields without neutralizing formula prefixes. A user who can create an expense with a description beginning with =, +, -, or @ can cause spreadsheet software to interpret the cell as a formula when a recipient opens the export. Quotes around the field do not reliably neutralize formula interpretation.

findings.title: Currency conversion accepts invalid rates and overflows amounts
findings.description: Currency creation and update store rateMicros directly from the request without requiring a positive bounded rate. convert() multiplies attacker-controlled/request-derived amountCents by source.rateMicros() in signed long arithmetic before division, so sufficiently large operands wrap and produce an incorrect or negative converted amount. A zero target rate also causes ArithmeticException. Managers can therefore corrupt conversion results used by clients; financial impact depends on downstream reliance on this endpoint's result.

findings.title: Purchase-order create and update accept caller-controlled status
findings.description: The POST and PUT /api/purchase-orders handlers pass the request DTO into PurchaseOrderMapper, which copies dto.status() directly into persisted records. PurchaseOrderService validates only the vendor reference and does not constrain status. Any authenticated user authorized to create or update their order can choose arbitrary states (including RECEIVED), bypassing the receive operation's intended OPEN-to-RECEIVED transition. This is workflow integrity tampering; no downstream financial processing was found in the reviewed scope.

findings.title: Purchase-order create/update accept caller-controlled status
findings.description: Any authenticated user can set the purchase-order workflow status directly during creation or update. PurchaseOrderService.validate only checks vendor tenancy, while PurchaseOrderMapper.create/apply copy dto.status() into the persisted entity. A caller can POST an order as RECEIVED (or set arbitrary states) or PUT an OPEN order to RECEIVED, bypassing the dedicated receive transition's OPEN-state check. This applies to POST /api/purchase-orders and PUT /api/purchase-orders/{id}; update still requires tenant and owner/manager authorization via require().

findings.title: Tax-rate calculation overflows for attacker-supplied amount
findings.description: Any authenticated tenant user can call GET /api/tax-rates/{id}/apply?amountCents=<long>. TaxRateService.apply multiplies amountCents by percentBp using signed long arithmetic before division; sufficiently large valid amounts overflow and return an incorrect (possibly negative) tax amount. This calculation is exposed directly by the controller and could corrupt downstream tax estimates.

findings.title: Webhook URL is accepted without restricting destination
findings.description: Webhook create/update accepts any non-empty URL via Text.required and stores it. This controller does not itself make an outbound request (ping only returns event/active), so SSRF is conditional on a delivery path using the stored URL; inspect delivery implementation before treating exploitation as established. Manager-level callers in a tenant can configure internal or otherwise sensitive destinations if a worker later delivers events to this URL.

findings.title: Mileage summary ignores manager-wide scope
findings.description: GET /api/mileage/summary uses the authenticated user's tenant to select entries but always filters to that user's ownerId. Unlike list(), which explicitly lets managers see tenant entries, the summary omits the manager condition and reports only the manager's own distance. This is an authorization/scope inconsistency causing incomplete aggregate data, not cross-tenant disclosure.

findings.title: Contracts and cost centers: no confirmed finding
findings.description: Scoped review of the contract and cost-center HTTP endpoints and service/repository paths found tenant-scoped reads and mutations. Contract endpoints require a manager via class-level method security; cost-center reads require authentication globally, and its writes require manager/admin. No confirmed security flaw in these groups.

findings.title: Notification routes enforce tenant and owner checks
findings.description: Reviewed all six notification route handlers and their complete service/mapper/repository path. GET list is constrained by tenant and owner; GET by id, PUT, DELETE, and POST read call requireOwn, which checks tenant and owner. POST create derives tenant and owner from authenticated AuthUser and only accepts subject/body/read from the DTO. No exploitable issue found in this route unit.

findings.description: No vulnerability identified; not saving as a finding. Policy controller gates all endpoints with @access.isManager(), and service scopes lookup and listing to authenticated user's tenant. Creation and updates preserve tenantId and ownerId from trusted current user/current record.

findings.title: Mileage entries accept negative distances, enabling summary tampering

findings.title: Policy records can be deleted by another manager in the same tenant

This is reachable through the API and allows same-tenant manager-level destructive modification of policies.

findings.title: Purchase order owner can set arbitrary lifecycle status

This bypasses the lifecycle guard; downstream status-dependent behavior is not established in this scoped code.

findings.title: Purchase-order status can be set through create/update payload
findings.description: Authenticated callers can supply the DTO status field to POST /api/purchase-orders or PUT /api/purchase-orders/{id}. PurchaseOrderMapper.create copies dto.status() into the new entity, and apply copies dto.status() into the existing entity without checking allowed transitions. A caller can set an order directly to RECEIVED (or another arbitrary status), bypassing the receive endpoint's OPEN-only transition. Ownership/tenant checks still apply to update, so the integrity issue is limited to orders the caller may create or edit.

findings.title: Tax application overflows long arithmetic
findings.description: GET /api/tax-rates/{id}/apply accepts caller-controlled amountCents as any long, then TaxRateService.apply multiplies it by the stored percentBp before division. Java long multiplication silently wraps. For example with a 10000 bp rate and amountCents=9223372036854775807, the intermediate wraps to -10000 and the returned taxCents is -1 rather than a positive amount. This permits callers to obtain materially incorrect tax results; rate creation/update accepts any int percentBp as well.

findings.title: Reminder snooze overflows dates for large dueOn values

The code accepts dueOn at creation/update without bounds and calls base.plusDays(days), causing DateTimeException for days 1–30. This makes that reminder's snooze action fail with a server error; it does not alter other reminders or bypass authorization.

findings.title: Tax calculation accepts negative and unbounded amounts
findings.description: The authenticated apply endpoint passes caller-controlled amountCents directly into multiplication without validating nonnegative amount or overflow; long arithmetic can wrap, producing incorrect tax results. findings.title: Cross-user read access to owner-scoped organization records

findings.title: Epic routes allow members to modify other users’ epics

findings.title: Task watcher endpoint exposes watcher lists for private tasks across the organization

findings.title: Internal export returns project data without per-project authorization

findings.title: Internal project export bypasses project authorization

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint bypasses tenant authorization

findings.title: Timesheet updates allow cross-org row reassignment

findings.title: API-key update mass-assigns organization and ownership fields
findings.description: PUT /api/api-keys/:id parses only label and scope, and apiKeyService.update passes that input to the repository. For a member, requireWritable checks the existing row's ownerId, then Table.update spreads the patch over the row. However this route does not accept caller-supplied ownerId/orgId because parseApiKeyInput constructs a new object with only label/scope. No mass-assignment flaw; do not report.

findings.title: Attachment filenames allow path traversal outside upload directory
findings.description: An authenticated user able to upload an attachment to a task they can access can supply a filename containing path separators and parent components. attachmentService only applies cleanName, which removes markup characters but preserves `/` and `..`; storage.put joins that value into the target and writes it without containment validation. The resulting target can escape UPLOAD_ROOT and overwrite files writable by the process.

findings.title: Attachment upload filename enables path traversal writes
findings.description: An authenticated user who can upload an attachment to a task in their organisation controls `input.filename`. `cleanName` removes markup characters but retains `/`, `\` and `..`; the resulting name is appended to the storage key and passed to `storage.put`, which joins it to `UPLOAD_ROOT` and writes the supplied content. A filename such as `../../../../target` can escape the upload directory (depending on the configured root/depth) and overwrite or create files writable by the service account.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-supplied organization header
findings.description: GET /api/billing/plan and /api/billing/invoices use X-Org-Id directly when present instead of verifying that it matches the authenticated user's organization. Billing routes are mounted after authenticate/securityRules but before resolveOrg, so resolveOrg's mismatch rejection does not protect them. Any authenticated manager or admin can supply another organization's ID and read its plan/payment-method last four digits or invoice summaries. GET /api/billing/usage correctly uses the authenticated user's orgId and is not affected.

findings.title: Cross-organization comment disclosure in search
findings.description: An authenticated user searching for a term receives matching comments from every organization. searchService scopes task and project matches to user.orgId, but commentRepo.search filters only by body text; returned comment bodies and task IDs therefore disclose other organizations' data. Trigger: call GET /api/search?q=<term of at least two characters> as a user in one organization when another organization's comment contains that term.

findings.title: Dashboard and epic records expose passcode through list/detail responses
findings.description: Dashboard and epic handlers serialize repository model rows directly. Their service list and require methods return the entire row, while the model records include owner and organization metadata; these models do not contain passcode. No sensitive field evident here; this finding is not warranted.

findings.title: Default service token protects internal API
findings.description: The /api/internal mount is gated only by requireServiceToken. env.serviceToken defaults to the hard-coded value "svc-dev-token" when SERVICE_TOKEN is unset. Any caller knowing that value passes the timing-safe equality check and can request arbitrary invoice IDs or project exports. Invoice/export handlers do not enforce org ownership; invoice responses include internalNote and exports include project task notes. Exploitation requires deployment without SERVICE_TOKEN configured and reachable API.

findings.title: Internal invoice endpoint exposes full invoice records to service-token callers
findings.description: GET /api/internal/invoices/:id passes the caller-controlled id to invoiceService.getById, which only checks existence and returns the complete invoice, including customer, amount, line items and internalNote. Unlike normal invoice routes, it has no organization ownership check. Any caller with the shared internal service token can retrieve any invoice by id.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint leaks cross-organization invoice data
findings.description: Any authenticated API user who can guess or obtain an invoice ID can request GET /api/invoices/:id/pdf and receive the invoice contents, including customer, line items, total, and internalNote, regardless of organization. The sibling invoice detail route uses invoiceService.get(user,id), which enforces invoice.orgId === user.orgId; the PDF route bypasses it and pdfService.render only checks that the ID exists.

findings.title: Project task endpoints expose private task contents to all org members
findings.description: Any authenticated user in the project's organization can request GET /api/projects/:id/tasks (and GET /api/tasks?projectId=...) and receive every top-level task, including tasks marked private and their notes. listForProject validates only that the project belongs to the user's org, then returns the repository's full project list without filtering task visibility or checking task ownership. The seeded private task includes confidential notes, confirming sensitive fields are returned.

findings.title: Public board export exposes private project task data
findings.description: GET /public/boards/:slug/export is unauthenticated (mounted before the /api authenticate middleware). The route checks only that the board exists and is published, then passes its projectId to exportProject. That service exports every top-level task, including notes and visibility, without filtering to public tasks. Anyone who knows a published board slug can retrieve private task content and metadata.

findings.title: Public registration grants manager access without verification or invitation
findings.description: The unauthenticated /api/auth/register endpoint creates a new organization and immediately assigns the caller a manager role. There is no invite, verification, or restriction on who may register. This lets any remote caller create privileged tenant accounts; impact is confined to the new org unless other cross-tenant access flaws exist.

findings.title: Published board export exposes private project tasks
findings.description: An unauthenticated caller can fetch `/public/boards/:slug/export` for any published board. The handler resolves the board's project and passes it to exportProject; exportProject includes every project task's title, notes, status, and visibility without filtering private tasks. Tasks default to private in taskService.create, so publishing a board can expose task contents not intended for public viewing.

findings.title: Search exposes comments across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated user searching for any term of at least two characters receives matching comments from every organization. searchService passes the raw query to commentRepo.search(q), whose predicate filters only comment body and never orgId. The response includes comment body and taskId, so a member can enumerate another tenant's matching comments.

findings.title: Task history exposes activity across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated caller can request GET /api/tasks/:id/history with a task ID from another organization. Unlike the other task operations, this handler passes the unvalidated ID directly to activityService.forEntity, whose repository filters only by entity and entityId and does not check orgId or task ownership. The response includes activity actor IDs, actions, timestamps, and details.

findings.title: Task move permits cross-organization reassignment
findings.description: A member can move a task they own into any project by supplying its projectId. move() checks ownership of the task via requireWritable(), but then loads the target project globally and only checks existence, before updating both projectId and orgId to target values. This bypasses projectService.require()'s organization check and transfers task data across organizations. Trigger: authenticated member POST /api/tasks/:id/move with owned task id and another organization's projectId.

findings.title: Automation reads expose every organization automation to members
findings.description: The automation list and per-ID GET return organization automation records without owner/role filtering. The ID parameter checks existence and organization membership, but not ownership. Authenticated members can enumerate automation names, triggers and enabled state across their organization. Writes are separately restricted to owner or non-member roles.

findings.title: Automation update permits cross-owner field overwrite through mass assignment
findings.description: Automation writes are allowed to any non-member role or the owner. The route parses only name, trigger, enabled, but automationService.update passes that input to the repository, and Table.update spreads arbitrary patch fields over the stored object. Since JavaScript object values can carry extra properties only if parser strips them (it does, constructing a fixed object), mass assignment is not evidenced here. No finding recorded.

findings.title: Comment creation allows spoofing the author ID
findings.description: An authenticated caller who can access a task can POST /api/tasks/:id/comments with an arbitrary authorId. The route initializes authorId from the authenticated user, then spreads req.body afterward, so the supplied field overrides it before commentService.add persists the object. This lets callers attribute comments to another user, corrupting audit/identity data and potentially impersonating users in comment listings.

findings.title: Cross-tenant API-key listing exposes organization credentials metadata
findings.description: GET /api/api-keys lists all rows for user.orgId. Unlike dashboard writes, API keys are org-scoped and list returns all keys regardless of owner; individual API key records include labels/scopes. Members can therefore enumerate metadata for keys belonging to other users in the same org. The route is authenticated and resolveOrg limits the org, so impact is confined to organization-level metadata disclosure.

findings.title: Internal project export has no project-level authorization
findings.description: Any caller with the shared internal service token can request an export for an arbitrary projectId. exportProject loads the project by ID and returns project/task data, including task notes, without checking caller authorization; its comment says callers are expected to authorize access, but this route performs no such check. A token-bearing integration can therefore retrieve projects outside its authorized scope.

findings.title: Notification GET exposes other users' notifications within an organization
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can request GET /api/notifications/:id for any notification in that organization. The id parameter loader checks only existence and orgId; the GET handler returns res.locals.row without checking ownerId or role. This bypasses the ownership checks present on notification writes and exposes notification title/channel and metadata to org members.

findings.title: Public invoice share token exposes full invoice data
findings.description: GET /public/invoices/:token is unauthenticated. Anyone holding the signed, unexpired share token receives invoice number, customer, amount, status, and all lines. The token is the sole access control; this is by design for sharing, but the endpoint exposes sensitive invoice data to any bearer and no further audience restriction exists. Token issuance is restricted to managers by POST /api/invoices/:id/share.

findings.title: Task history endpoint leaks cross-organization activity
findings.description: An authenticated user can request `/api/tasks/:id/history` using a task ID from another organization. The route calls activityService.forEntity directly without first calling taskService.require, and forEntity queries by entity/entityId only with no organization check. Activity rows contain actorId, action, detail, and timestamps.

findings.title: Template reads disclose full organization templates to members
findings.description: All authenticated callers can list and read template records in their organization. Template service's requireWritable protects mutations only; list and require have no role/ownership filter. A member can enumerate other users' template names and bodies through GET /api/templates and GET /api/templates/:id. This is an org-scoped confidentiality issue; other organizations remain blocked by orgId checks.

findings.title: Timesheets expose every organization member's entries
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can enumerate all timesheet rows and fetch another member's row by ID. The GET collection returns timesheetService.list(org), which filters only by org; GET /:id checks only that the row belongs to the active org and never checks ownership or role. This discloses coworkers' week and hours data. The organization boundary is enforced, but there is no per-owner/role boundary.

findings.title: Webhook delivery endpoint exposes stored bearer credentials
findings.description: An authenticated organization member can request GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. The service checks only that the webhook belongs to the member's organization, then returns stored delivery records in full. WebhookDelivery.requestHeaders contains Authorization bearer tokens (as shown by seeded deliveries), giving members the secret used to authenticate to webhook consumers. The endpoint is registered before the manager-role middleware.

findings.title: Integration link reads disclose org-wide link records to members
findings.description: Integration link GET/list permit any authenticated organization member to read link metadata for the organization. The service scopes by orgId but has no role or owner check for reads. Integration link records contain provider and externalId (per model/input), not credentials or tokens in the inspected flow. This is limited to metadata disclosure; mutations are restricted to non-member roles.

findings.title: Authenticated users can escalate roles through admin API
findings.description: Admin endpoints are protected by URL rule /api/admin/*, but Spring's single-segment wildcard does not match nested paths such as /api/admin/users/{id}/roles. These nested endpoints fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). AdminService checks only tenant equality for role changes and deactivation, not that actor is an administrator. Any authenticated tenant user can promote themselves to ADMIN (or SERVICE) and deactivate peers.

findings.title: Cross-tenant project transfer exposes expenses to target tenant
findings.description: A manager authorized for a source project can transfer its expenses to any project ID, including a project belonging to another tenant. The target is fetched globally without checking its tenant, and ExpenseRepository.reassign changes only projectId, retaining the original expense tenant. The destination tenant can then retrieve those foreign expenses through GET /api/projects/{targetId}/expenses, which filters by project ID without tenant filtering.

findings.title: Global search returns comments across tenant boundaries
findings.description: GlobalSearchService scopes expenses and vendors to the authenticated tenant, but searches every comment in CommentRepository and returns matching bodies without checking comment tenant or expense ownership. Any authenticated user can query a distinctive substring and receive comments from other tenants (and comments on other users' expenses).

findings.title: Public statement endpoint accepts any valid share token for any statement ID
findings.description: The public share handler validates that a token is a share token but discards its embedded statement subject, then builds the statement identified by the independent path parameter. Consequently, possession of a share link for one statement authorizes retrieval of any other statement when its ID is known or guessed.

findings.title: Vendor bank details replacement lacks manager/tenant authorization
findings.description: The PUT bank-details endpoint omits the @PreAuthorize tenant-manager check used by adjacent vendor endpoints. Its service trusts the caller-supplied tenantId to locate and overwrite a vendor's bank details; there is no tenant equality or role check in replaceBankDetails. Any authenticated user can modify bank account details across tenants by supplying a target tenantId and vendor ID.

findings.title: Receipt download bypasses expense and tenant authorization
findings.description: The download route accepts only receiptId and directly loads and returns the receipt. Unlike receipt list/describe/remove routes, it does not authorize the user against the associated expense or tenant. Any authenticated user able to obtain or guess a receipt ID can retrieve its contents across tenants.

findings.title: API-key rotation uses predictable sequence values
findings.description: An authenticated owner can rotate a key through POST /api/api-keys/{id}/rotate. ApiKeyService.rotate constructs the new key material from Ids.next(), whose implementation uses a process-wide AtomicLong counter starting at 1000 (see common/Ids.java:7,13). The returned DTO includes that generated string in prefix, and the persisted key record uses it. Subsequent values are sequential and guessable, so an attacker who can infer the counter can forge/guess key material. The review is static; actual use of this stored field for API-key authentication is outside the assigned files and was not verified.

findings.title: Billing endpoints allow authenticated users to query another tenant
findings.description: The billing controller accepts X-Tenant-Id as the tenant selector and passes it directly to the service. TenantFilter explicitly skips every /api/billing route, so its comparison against the authenticated user's tenant never runs. The repository then returns the plan or invoices for whichever tenant ID is supplied. Any authenticated user can therefore read cross-tenant subscription and invoice data.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-supplied tenant ID
findings.description: Any authenticated caller can choose X-Tenant-Id on /api/billing/plan or /api/billing/invoices. BillingService forwards that value directly to repository lookups without comparing it to the authenticated principal's tenant. A caller who knows or guesses another tenant ID can read its subscription and invoice records.

findings.title: Export name allows path traversal and arbitrary file overwrite
findings.description: Any authenticated caller able to create an export controls request.name. Text.plain only strips markup and whitespace; it does not remove path separators or dot segments. Resolving name + ".csv" against exportDir therefore allows values such as ../../somefile to escape the export directory, and Files.writeString truncates/overwrites the resolved target. Impact depends on service filesystem permissions and writable target paths.

findings.title: Global search returns cross-tenant comments
findings.description: The authenticated /api/search?q=... route adds every matching comment returned by CommentRepository.search(q) to the response without tenant or ownership filtering. CommentRepository.search scans the entire in-memory comment store. A user can search for a term present in another tenant's comment and receive its body and ID.

findings.title: Project expense transfer permits cross-tenant reassignment
findings.description: An authenticated project manager can call POST /api/projects/{sourceId}/transfer-expenses with a targetProjectId belonging to another tenant. The source is checked against the caller's tenant, but target lookup uses unrestricted findById and never checks the target tenant. ExpenseRepository.reassign then changes every source expense to the foreign project ID. This writes one tenant's expense records into another tenant's project association.

findings.title: Public receipt download bypasses expense authorization
findings.description: GET /api/receipts/{receiptId}/download has no authenticated principal and calls ReceiptService.load directly, which looks up receipt by ID without checking tenant or owning expense. Any caller who obtains/guesses a receipt ID can retrieve stored receipt bytes; controller also uses attacker-supplied stored contentType and filename in response headers.

findings.title: Service-role comment relay trusts caller-supplied tenant and author identifiers
findings.description: The service-role-only POST /api/integrations/comments accepts CommentInput and passes it straight to CommentService.add. That service persists the supplied tenantId, expenseId and authorId without verifying that the expense belongs to the stated tenant or that the author is authorized. Any caller with a SERVICE credential can forge comments attributed to arbitrary users and attach them to arbitrary expense IDs, including another tenant's records.

findings.title: Statement share token is not bound to requested statement
findings.description: GET /public/statements/{id}?token=... checks only that token subject() returns some valid stmt token, then builds the statement named by the independent path id. A valid share token issued for statement A can therefore authorize access to any statement B if its ID is known. StatementService.build performs no authorization by design.

findings.title: Tenant members can invoke admin mutation methods
findings.description: The admin mutation service methods enforce tenant isolation but never require an administrator role. AdminUserController.changeRole/deactivate pass the authenticated principal directly to these methods, which only verify target tenant equality before saving. The nested mutation routes are not protected by a controller-level role annotation. Because the security configuration's /api/admin/* matcher covers only one path segment, these nested routes fall through to authenticated-only access. Any authenticated user in a tenant can assign roles (including ADMIN), deactivate users, or update tenant limits.

findings.title: Vendor bank details can be changed by any authenticated tenant user
findings.description: The bank-details PUT handler has no @PreAuthorize unlike every neighboring vendor endpoint. Global security only requires authentication, and replaceBankDetails checks that a vendor exists in the supplied tenant but does not check the caller's role. Any authenticated USER in their own tenant can overwrite the vendor's account name, IBAN and BIC; these fields drive vendor payment details, so this permits payment redirection. The tenant-path comparison prevents cross-tenant writes for non-SERVICE users only insofar as their actual vendor ownership is checked, but it does not enforce manager authorization.

findings.title: Zero currency rate causes conversion endpoint failure
findings.description: A manager can create or update a tenant currency with rateMicros=0 because CurrencyMapper accepts the DTO value without validation. CurrencyService.convert divides by the target rate at line 43; requesting that currency as `to` triggers ArithmeticException and a failed conversion request. This is request-scoped failure rather than service-wide outage.

findings.title: Review of authentication, tenant context, token signing and global route controls
findings.description: No confirmed vulnerability identified within the assigned security/configuration/global-entry-point scope. The bearer filter accepts only signed payloads that resolve to active users; tenant filter rejects mismatched X-Tenant-Id for non-SERVICE principals and clears thread-local state in finally. Token signing uses HMAC-SHA256 with constant-time signature comparison and generates a random 32-byte key when no configured secret is present. SecurityConfig requires SERVICE for internal/integration paths, ADMIN for /api/admin/* and authentication otherwise, with only health/status/public paths permitted anonymously.

findings.title: Export name allows path traversal and arbitrary CSV file overwrite
findings.description: An authenticated user can submit an export name containing path separators or an absolute path. ExportService applies Text.plain, which removes markup/normalizes whitespace but does not constrain path components, then resolves name + ".csv" against exportDir. Path.resolve accepts traversal and absolute paths, so Files.writeString can overwrite any file writable by the service whose resolved path ends in .csv. The later download filename is sanitized, but that does not constrain the write target.

findings.title: Global search returns comments across tenant boundaries

GlobalSearchService.search calls comments.search(q) without a tenant or ownership constraint and serializes each matching comment body into SearchHit. CommentRepository.search scans all comments, so a query of at least three characters can disclose matching comments from other tenants regardless of the user's tenant or role.

findings.title: Nested admin routes bypass admin role matcher
findings.description: The security configuration protects only paths matching `/api/admin/*` with ADMIN authority, while admin mutation routes are nested more deeply (`/api/admin/users/{id}/roles`, `/deactivate`, `/api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits`). These do not match the single-segment pattern and fall through to `anyRequest().authenticated()`. The service methods enforce tenant equality but never require an admin/manager role. Any authenticated user can therefore change a same-tenant user's role (including promoting them to ADMIN), deactivate users, and update tenant limits. Confirm exact Spring matcher semantics in deployed framework/runtime remains untested; source shows the mismatch.

findings.title: Project expense transfer accepts a cross-tenant destination
findings.description: A manager of a source project can POST /api/projects/{sourceId}/transfer-expenses with any existing project ID as targetProjectId. The service checks the source is managed and checks only that the target exists; it never applies requireInTenant to the target or compares tenant IDs. ExpenseRepository.reassign rewrites each moved expense's projectId without changing its tenantId. This allows cross-tenant expense reassignment, causing destination-side project expense listings to include expenses from another tenant and corrupting tenant/project associations.

findings.title: Public statement endpoint ignores share-token subject
findings.description: PublicStatementController validates that the supplied share token is valid but discards its subject, then returns the statement selected by the independent path id. A valid share token issued for one statement therefore authorizes access to any statement whose id is known or guessed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated receipt download exposes tenant receipt content
findings.description: The download endpoint accepts a receipt ID without an AuthUser and calls ReceiptService.load directly. That method performs only a global repository lookup, with no tenant, ownership, or authentication check. Any authenticated principal (the route requires authentication globally) who obtains/guesses a receipt ID can download its content across tenants; the sequential/predictable nature of IDs requires checking Ids implementation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated tenant-scoped billing data exposure
findings.description: The billing controller accepts an arbitrary tenant ID from X-Tenant-Id. SecurityConfig requires only authentication for /api/billing, while TenantFilter explicitly exempts all /api/billing paths. Neither controller nor BillingService binds the requested tenant to the authenticated principal. Any authenticated user can therefore read another tenant's plan and invoices, including invoice amounts and status.

findings.title: Unbounded currency rate and amount permit overflow and division by zero
findings.description: An authenticated caller can invoke GET /api/currencies/convert with amount, from, and to. Currency rates are accepted from manager-controlled DTOs without positivity or bounds validation; convert multiplies attacker-influenced amountCents by source.rateMicros() using long arithmetic and divides by target.rateMicros(). A target rate of zero triggers ArithmeticException (request failure); large values wrap and produce an incorrect signed conversion result. This can corrupt financial calculations and reliably cause request errors for a tenant when a zero-rate currency is configured.

findings.title: Tax rate arithmetic overflows for large amount inputs
findings.description: The public GET /api/tax-rates/{id}/apply endpoint accepts any signed long amountCents and computes amountCents * percentBp in long arithmetic before dividing by 10000. There is no range validation; sufficiently large values overflow and return an incorrect tax amount. This endpoint is read-only, but wrong tax computation can corrupt downstream decisions if callers rely on the result.

findings.title: API-key write endpoints allow any authenticated user to create, change, rotate, or delete own keys
findings.description: Potentially no finding: API keys are deliberately per-user and writes are allowed to the owner; code enforces requireOwn on operations by id. Any authenticated user creating their own key may be intended. Do not record absent evidence of impact.

findings.title: Budget API lets callers set authoritative spentCents
findings.description: Authenticated users can POST or PUT a budget with an arbitrary spentCents value. BudgetMapper.create copies dto.spentCents() into the persisted Budget, and BudgetMapper.apply does the same on update; the controller accepts the DTO directly. The resulting remaining endpoint returns limitCents - spentCents without recomputation. An owner can therefore falsify their budget utilization/remaining balance; managers can do so for any budget in their tenant. The default-enabled demo data is not required for this behavior.

findings.title: Card update permits owner to change frozen state
findings.description: Any card owner can PUT /api/cards/{id} and CardMapper.apply copies dto.frozen into the persisted card. Unlike the dedicated freeze action, this permits an owner to unfreeze a card (or freeze it) through general update, bypassing any intended freeze-state transition controls. The card ownership check does not distinguish this field.

findings.title: Comment creation trusts caller-supplied authorId
findings.description: An authenticated user can POST a comment for an expense they can access, but the controller only replaces tenantId and expenseId. CommentInput.forExpense preserves the request body's authorId, and CommentService persists it as the comment author. A caller can therefore attribute comments to another user, undermining authorship/audit attribution.

findings.title: Comment creation trusts caller-supplied authorId
findings.description: An authenticated user can submit POST /api/expenses/{expenseId}/comments with CommentInput.authorId set to another user's ID. CommentController validates access to the expense, then forExpense only replaces tenantId and expenseId while preserving authorId; CommentService stores that ID as the comment author. This permits forged attribution in tenant-visible comment records.

findings.title: Expense descriptions in exports can trigger spreadsheet formula injection
findings.description: An authenticated expense owner or manager can place spreadsheet formula syntax in an expense description. ExportService quotes the description as a CSV field and replaces double quotes, but does not neutralize formula-leading characters. When a recipient opens the downloaded CSV in spreadsheet software, the description may be evaluated as a formula, potentially enabling data access or actions supported by that spreadsheet.

findings.title: Expense details and draft operations ignore owner role for managers
findings.description: ExpenseService.get requires only same-tenant access and owner-or-manager access. Since managers pass that guard for every owner, manager callers can view, update, submit, and delete another employee's draft. This exposes and permits manipulation of tenant expense data; it may be intentional for review workflows, but the submit/delete paths also apply to drafts without an explicit ownership distinction.

findings.title: Per diem entries accept unchecked negative days and rates
findings.description: Authenticated tenant users can POST or PUT a PerDiemDto with negative days or rateCents, or arbitrarily large values. PerDiemMapper.create/apply only require a non-empty destination and copy these numeric fields directly into the record; the service persists them. This permits malformed or manipulated per-diem amounts in tenant records and can corrupt downstream expense totals/reports that consume these values. No numeric validation was found in this unit's path.

findings.title: Purchase-order create/update accept caller-controlled status transitions
findings.description: An authenticated tenant user can submit an arbitrary `status` in the PurchaseOrderDto on create or update. PurchaseOrderMapper.create copies dto.status() directly into the new record (line 20), and apply copies it directly into the replacement record (line 26); PurchaseOrderService.create/update call those mapper methods after validating only vendorRef (service lines 35–43, 67–71). Thus callers can create an order already marked RECEIVED or change an existing order's status without using the receive operation's OPEN-state check. Owner/tenant authorization remains enforced for updates, but does not constrain status transitions.

findings.title: Tag attachment endpoint exposes cross-tenant expense existence via failure behavior
findings.description: POST /api/tags/{id}/attach/{expenseId} verifies the tag belongs to the caller's tenant and that the caller owns the tag or is a manager, then calls expenses.get(user, expenseId) before attaching. This path appears properly tenant-scoped if ExpenseService.get enforces tenant ownership; inspect that service behavior before asserting an issue.
