VendorService.require constrains the vendor lookup to that supplied tenant, but does not bind it to the caller's tenant or role.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-supplied tenant ID
findings.description: Both billing routes require authentication globally but are exempted from TenantFilter, then pass the raw X-Tenant-Id header through BillingService to repositories. Any authenticated principal can request another tenant's subscription or invoices, disclosing plan, seat and invoice/payment-status details. Trigger: authenticate as a user of t-alpha and GET /api/billing/invoices with X-Tenant-Id: t-bravo (or request /plan).

findings.title: Billing routes trust caller-supplied tenant ID
findings.description: Both billing endpoints accept X-Tenant-Id as the tenant selector and pass it directly to the service. TenantFilter explicitly skips every /api/billing request (TenantFilter.java:19-21), while SecurityConfig only requires authentication for these routes and applies no billing-specific role restriction. Any authenticated user can therefore request another tenant's subscription and invoice records by changing the header.

findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver identity
findings.description: The manager-only bulk-approval endpoint passes request.approverId() into the decision logic instead of the authenticated actor's id. The self-approval guard compares the expense requester against that client-controlled value, so a manager who submitted an expense can approve it by supplying any other approverId. The chosen identity is also persisted as decidedBy and written to the audit entry, enabling forged attribution.

findings.title: Expense reassignment trusts a project ID outside the caller's tenant
findings.description: An authenticated user can create or update an expense while supplying any project ID belonging to another tenant if that project is resolvable. The service verifies only that the referenced project's tenant matches the user's tenant, which is correct. Wait—this condition blocks the cross-tenant project reference, so no finding here.

findings.title: Export name permits path traversal and file overwrite
findings.description: An authenticated caller can submit an export name containing path separators and `..`. `Text.plain` only strips markup/normalizes whitespace, so `ExportService.create` resolves `name + ".csv"` beneath `exportDir` without normalizing or constraining it. `Files.writeString` then follows traversal components and overwrites a path outside the export directory if the service account can write it. This is a file-system integrity issue; reach requires authenticated access and a writable target with the `.csv` suffix.

findings.title: Global search leaks comments across tenants
findings.description: An authenticated user can search comments belonging to any tenant. GlobalSearchService passes only the query to CommentRepository.search and returns every matching comment body without filtering by tenant, expense ownership, or role. Comment records carry tenantId and expenseId, while /api/search is authenticated by the API security chain. A query of at least three characters matching another tenant's comment exposes its content and ID.

findings.title: Global search returns comments across tenant and owner boundaries
findings.description: An authenticated user can call GET /api/search?q=<three-or-more-character-query>. GlobalSearchService scopes expenses by tenant and owner, but passes the query to CommentRepository.search, which searches every stored comment without tenant, expense-visibility, or author checks. Results include other tenants' comment bodies and IDs; ordinary users also receive comments on records they cannot access.

findings.title: Nested admin user endpoints omit the admin authorization check
findings.description: Authenticated users can reach nested role/deactivation operations because SecurityConfig restricts only /api/admin/* (one path segment), while the nested controller routes /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and /deactivate have no method-level role guard. AdminService then trusts the supplied target ID and permits same-tenant role changes, including promotion to ADMIN. This crosses authorization boundaries within a tenant and can grant administrative control.

findings.title: Project transfer can reassign expenses to a different tenant's project
findings.description: A manager of a source project can submit a targetProjectId for a project in another tenant. The service verifies the source project is managed by the caller, but loads target by id and never checks its tenant. It then reassigns every source expense to that target id, crossing the tenant boundary and corrupting tenant association. Trigger: POST /api/projects/{sourceId}/transfer-expenses with a cross-tenant targetProjectId.

findings.title: Receipt download omits tenant and expense authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated user who knows or guesses a receiptId can download its bytes. ReceiptController.download calls receipts.load(receiptId) without an AuthUser or expenseId; ReceiptService.load performs only a repository lookup. By contrast, list/describe/remove first call ExpenseService.get, which enforces tenant and owner-or-manager access. The security filter requires authentication but does not authorize the receipt's tenant or owner.

findings.title: Saved-filter IDs collide across tenants, allowing cross-tenant overwrite and deletion
findings.description: SavedFilterRepository stores records in a global map keyed only by id. SavedFilterMapper.create uses generated IDs, but create saves with store.put(entity.id(), entity), replacing an existing tenant's record if an ID collides. More directly, concurrent/otherwise duplicate IDs across tenants let a tenant's create overwrite another tenant's filter; the original tenant then cannot retrieve it. Deletion uses removeInTenant after lookup but map state can race. Main concern depends on ID generator collision; inspect Ids for entropy. No confirmed exploitable issue yet.

findings.title: Share-token endpoint accepts any valid token for arbitrary statement ID
findings.description: The public statement handler verifies that the supplied token is signed and has a `stmt:` payload, but discards the payload and calls `service.build(id)` using the independent path parameter. `StatementService.build` performs no authorization (its comment says callers are responsible), so a valid share token for one statement can be paired with another statement ID to retrieve that statement's full view. Trigger: GET /public/statements/{victimId}?token=<valid-share-token-for-other-statement>.

findings.title: Tenant users can invoke administrative mutations
findings.description: Any authenticated user in a tenant can change another same-tenant user's role, deactivate them, or alter tenant limits. SecurityConfig protects only the single-segment pattern /api/admin/*; nested mutation URLs such as /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and /api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). AdminService then checks tenant equality but never requires manager/admin authority. A normal USER can promote themselves or another tenant user to ADMIN and disable accounts.

findings.title: Budget API lets callers set recorded spending
findings.description: POST /api/budgets and PUT /api/budgets/{id} accept BudgetDto with caller-controlled spentCents; BudgetMapper.create and apply copy that value directly into persisted Budget. A caller can create or modify an owned budget with an arbitrary spending total (including a negative amount), causing remainingCents to report manipulated values. This affects the caller's own budget; no cross-owner access was found.

findings.title: Budget API trusts client-supplied spent amounts
findings.description: An authenticated budget owner can submit or update a budget with any spentCents value. BudgetMapper.create and apply copy dto.spentCents() directly into persisted Budget, and remaining() uses that value to calculate remaining funds. A caller can therefore falsify budget utilization (including setting it negative or above the limit), with the endpoint returning the falsified remaining balance. Ownership checks restrict which existing budget can be changed but do not constrain this accounting field.

findings.title: Budget create/update lets callers forge spent amounts
findings.description: Authenticated budget owners can set spentCents directly when creating or updating their budgets; tenant managers can do so for any budget they own/manage. BudgetDto exposes spentCents and BudgetMapper.create/apply copies it without validation or derivation. This makes the remaining endpoint return caller-selected budget usage (limitCents - spentCents), undermining the integrity of budget tracking. No control in this package restricts spentCents to trusted transaction data or a valid range.

findings.title: Comment creation trusts client-supplied authorId
findings.description: An authenticated expense owner or manager can POST a comment with authorId naming another user. CommentController only replaces tenantId and expenseId via forExpense; CommentService persists the remaining authorId unchanged. This permits forged attribution in stored comments.

findings.title: CSV formula injection in expense exports
findings.description: An authenticated user can cause exported CSV descriptions to begin with spreadsheet formula characters (for example =, +, -, or @). ExportService.render encloses description in quotes but does not neutralize formula prefixes; spreadsheet applications may evaluate the cell when an authorized user opens the downloaded export. A trigger requires control of an expense description through the expense creation/update paths.

findings.title: Currency conversion permits zero rates and overflows
findings.description: An authenticated tenant user can call GET /api/currencies/convert with an amount long and tenant currency codes. CurrencyMapper.create/apply accepts rateMicros without a positive-value constraint, so a manager can store rateMicros=0 and trigger division-by-zero (request failure), or supply crafted rates/amounts that overflow signed long arithmetic and return an incorrect converted amount. This affects tenant conversion results; write routes are manager/admin protected.

findings.title: Project expense listing bypasses expense ownership checks
findings.description: Any authenticated user in a tenant who can read a project can retrieve every expense assigned to it, including expenses owned by other non-manager users. ExpenseService.list filters to owner unless manager, but ProjectService.expensesOf only checks project tenant membership before returning every matching expense. Trigger: GET /api/projects/{id}/expenses for a same-tenant project containing another user's expense.

findings.title: Tax calculation overflows for large amountCents
findings.description: An authenticated tenant user can call GET /api/tax-rates/{id}/apply with any long amountCents. TaxRateService multiplies the unbounded amount by percentBp in signed 64-bit arithmetic before dividing by 10000. Large valid long inputs overflow and return an incorrect taxCents value, potentially negative, rather than rejecting or calculating safely. The route scopes the rate to the caller's tenant, but does not bound the amount; percentBp is also accepted without range validation on create/update.

findings.description: This is an aggregate non-vulnerability record; inspected code paths showed controls for the object-level authorization risks in scope. No code changes made.

findings.title: No confirmed TagController vulnerability
findings.description: Reviewed all six mapped Tag route declarations. Tenant filtering, owner/manager mutation checks, DTO field selection, and expense authorization control the inspected paths; no exploitable issue was confirmed.

Any deployment that omits this environment variable has a publicly guessable credential for the internal endpoints, including invoice lookup, project export, and the Slack comment integration.

Any authenticated user can request another known org ID and retrieve its plan/payment-method suffix or invoice metadata.

findings.title: Cross-organization task move via unchecked destination project
findings.description: An authenticated member who owns a task can call POST /api/tasks/:id/move with a projectId belonging to another organization. The source task is checked against the caller's organization, but the destination is only checked for existence; the update then changes both projectId and orgId to the destination organization. This transfers the task and its notes/title across tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint omits organization authorization

Unlike neighboring invoice routes, this handler does not call invoiceService.get(who(req), id); it calls pdfService.render(id), which retrieves solely by ID and serializes customer, lines, total, and internalNote. The application authenticates /api routes but no ownership control is applied here.

findings.title: Passcodes stored with fast unsalted SHA-256
findings.description: Login and registration hash passcodes with a single unsalted SHA-256 digest. If a user table or backup is exposed, weak or reused passcodes can be recovered offline at high speed; the seeded passcodes are short and are direct targets. Replace with a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with per-record salts and suitable cost.

The route only checks that the board is published, then passes its projectId to exportProject, which returns every task in the project including IDs, notes, and visibility, unlike the public board view which filters to visibility === "public". A published board slug therefore grants access to non-public project content and task notes.

findings.title: Search results disclose comments across organizations

findings.title: Task history endpoint returns activity without checking task ownership

Unlike adjacent task subresource handlers, this handler passes the supplied ID directly to activityService.forEntity without calling taskService.require. That service filters only by entity and entityId, not orgId, and returns activity details, exposing cross-tenant task history.

Owner checks only restrict updates/deletes; read endpoints return all organization rows without owner-based filtering. This may be intentional for shared approval/timesheet visibility, but owner-specific policy is not enforced for reads.

findings.description: Unauthenticated GET /public/boards/:slug/export first checks only that the board is published, then passes its projectId to exportService.exportProject. findings.title: Slack comment integration trusts caller-supplied author identity
findings.description: POST /api/internal/integrations/slack/comments is reachable with the shared service token, but accepts authorEmail and taskId from the request body and creates a comment attributed to that user. The handler does not verify a Slack signature or bind the author to an authenticated Slack actor. Any holder of the service token can impersonate any existing user in the task's organization and post comments.

findings.title: Task history endpoint exposes activity records without organization check
findings.description: The authenticated task history route accepts an arbitrary task ID and queries activity by entity and entityId only. Unlike neighboring task endpoints, it does not first call taskService.require to ensure the task belongs to the caller's organization. The returned activity records can include actor IDs, action details, and timestamps from another organization's task.

findings.title: Task move permits cross-organization project reassignment
findings.description: An authenticated user who can write a task in their organization can move it to any project ID, including a project in another organization. move() verifies the task belongs to the caller via requireWritable(), but fetches the target with projectRepo.get() and checks only that it exists. It then overwrites the task's projectId and orgId with the target's values. This transfers the task and its contents across tenant boundaries; subsequent tenant queries may expose it to the destination organization.

findings.title: Timesheet creation lets input overwrite tenant and owner fields
findings.description: POST /api/timesheets passes caller input into create. The service constructs the row with trusted orgId and ownerId before spreading input, so extra JSON fields named orgId or ownerId overwrite those values. A member can create a timesheets row in another organization or assign it to another user; subsequent row access is gated only by orgId and writes by ownerId/role. This permits cross-org placement and ownership manipulation.

findings.title: Webhook delivery history exposes bearer auth tokens
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can request GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. The org ownership check is present, but the returned WebhookDelivery objects include requestHeaders, and seeded deliveries store Authorization: Bearer <webhook authToken>. A member can therefore retrieve the org's webhook credential and impersonate the webhook recipient-facing sender.

findings.title: Epics and templates: member can modify another user's objects in same org
findings.description: A member can update or delete any epic or template in their organization by supplying its ID. The services do enforce same-org isolation, but requireWritable blocks only when owner differs AND role is member. Because route handlers use these services directly, cross-owner same-org writes and deletes are reachable by authenticated members; templates archive has the same check.

findings.title: Milestone object reads are not restricted to the owner
findings.description: Any authenticated user whose active org contains a milestone can retrieve its full row via GET /api/milestones/:id. The id middleware only enforces organization equality, while GET returns res.locals.row without checking ownerId; member-level writes do check ownership.

findings.title: Task comment creation allows author impersonation
findings.description: An authenticated caller can submit POST /api/tasks/:id/comments with authorId set to another user. The route spreads req.body after authorId: user.id, and commentService.add persists the resulting input unchanged. The taskId and orgId are overwritten safely, but authorId is not, so comments can be falsely attributed to other users in that organization.

findings.title: Admin URL matcher leaves nested admin mutations available to any authenticated user
findings.description: The admin role matcher uses /api/admin/*, which only matches one path segment after /api/admin. Nested mutations such as PUT /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and PUT /api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). Their controllers have no method-level role guard, and AdminService only checks same-tenant membership, allowing an ordinary user to promote a same-tenant account to ADMIN or change limits.

findings.title: Authenticated users can download any tenant's receipt by receipt ID
findings.description: The receipt download handler accepts no authenticated principal or expense context and loads a receipt solely by caller-supplied receipt ID. The API security chain requires authentication, but there is no object-level tenant or ownership check, so any authenticated account with a receipt ID can retrieve its file contents.

findings.title: Billing endpoints expose tenant subscription and invoice data via caller-selected tenant header
findings.description: Authenticated callers choose X-Tenant-Id for plan and invoice queries. BillingController passes this untrusted value directly to BillingService, which queries solely by that tenant ID. TenantFilter explicitly skips /api/billing, so no tenant-header consistency check occurs. Any authenticated tenant user can request another tenant's subscription and invoices by changing the header.

findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver identity
findings.description: Bulk approval accepts an approverId from the request and uses it as the acting identity rather than deriving identity from the authenticated principal. The later self-approval guard checks that supplied value, allowing an authenticated approver to claim a different approver ID and bypass self-approval restrictions; records and audit entries are likewise attributed to the spoofed ID.

findings.title: Integration service can create arbitrary cross-tenant comments
findings.description: The service-role integration endpoint accepts tenantId, expenseId, and authorId from the request body and persists them directly. It does not verify the expense exists, belongs to tenantId, or that the service principal is authorized for that tenant. Any caller with a SERVICE token can inject comments into another tenant's expenses and spoof the author.

findings.title: Project expense transfer can move expenses into a different tenant's project
findings.description: The source project is manager-authorized, but target project is loaded globally without checking that it belongs to the actor's tenant or even the same tenant as the source. Expenses are reassigned to the target project ID while retaining their original tenant ID. A member of the target tenant can then retrieve those expenses through expensesOf, which filters by project ID and does not filter expense tenant, disclosing source-tenant expense details.

findings.title: Valid public share token can retrieve a different statement
findings.description: The public endpoint verifies that a token is valid but discards its embedded statement subject, then builds the statement selected by the caller-controlled path ID. A holder of any valid statement share token can therefore request a different known/guessed statement ID, bypassing the intended share scope and potentially crossing tenant boundaries.

If tenant IDs can contain path separators or traversal sequences, the request can write outside the intended template directory, with the service account's filesystem permissions. Any authenticated user can therefore overwrite bank account details for any vendor if they know its tenant and vendor IDs.

Although this service's `rotate` generates a fresh prefix, creation and update do not. This allows an authenticated owner to set or overwrite the key credential value rather than a display-only prefix, potentially enabling self-selected/reused credentials if this field is consumed as an API key by other code. In the reviewed caller scope no API-key authentication consumer was identified, so security impact of the stored value is not established; do not treat as confirmed exploitable credential forgery.

findings.title: Budget owners can forge spent amounts
findings.description: The budget create and update routes accept BudgetDto values and BudgetMapper copies dto.spentCents() directly into the stored Budget (create lines 18-21; apply lines 24-28). Any authenticated budget owner can therefore submit arbitrary positive, negative, or extreme spentCents values. The remaining endpoint returns limitCents minus this attacker-controlled value (BudgetService lines 43-45), so callers can falsify remaining budget figures; integrity impact depends on downstream reliance on that figure.

findings.title: Currency conversion accepts zero rates and overflows long arithmetic

The submitted expense then reaches ApprovalService, allowing negative-value expenses into the approval workflow and potentially corrupting downstream financial totals.

This enables attribution spoofing in comment history. The integration endpoint similarly accepts the supplied authorId but is restricted to SERVICE role.

findings.title: Demo-data toggle seeds predictable demo identities and records
findings.description: The application.yml defaults ledger.demo-data to true, activating DemoDataLoader on normal startup unless explicitly overridden. The loader creates active admin and manager accounts for two tenants and seeds sensitive sample records. Authentication token issuing is not exposed by the reviewed code, so exploitability depends on another way to obtain a valid token; this is a risky production default rather than demonstrated unauthenticated access.

findings.title: Exported expense descriptions permit spreadsheet formula injection
findings.description: A tenant user can create or edit an expense description beginning with spreadsheet formula syntax (for example =HYPERLINK(...)); ExpenseMapper stores the description after Text.required, which strips markup/normalizes whitespace but does not neutralize formula characters. ExportService.render places the description in a quoted CSV field, replacing double quotes but leaving leading =, +, -, or @ untouched. Opening the downloaded CSV in a spreadsheet may evaluate the cell as a formula. Any export consumer who opens attacker-controlled expense data is exposed.

findings.title: Negative expense amounts can be submitted for approval
findings.description: An authenticated expense creator can send an ExpenseDto with amountCents below zero. ExpenseMapper.create copies the value without validation, and ExpenseService.submit changes a draft to SUBMITTED and opens an approval. This lets a tenant user introduce negative-value expenses into the approval workflow; no amount constraint appears on these paths.

findings.title: Purchase order status is caller-controlled on create and update
findings.description: Authenticated users can supply arbitrary purchase-order status in the DTO. PurchaseOrderMapper.create copies dto.status() into the new entity, and apply copies dto.status() into the existing entity; PurchaseOrderService.validate checks only vendorRef. Consequently a caller can create an order already marked RECEIVED or update an OPEN order directly to RECEIVED (or any other value), bypassing the receive endpoint's OPEN-state check and the intended state transition. The receive route itself checks OPEN before setting RECEIVED, but that control is bypassed by create/update.

findings.title: Webhook manager authorization is not tenant-scoped
findings.description: Every /api/webhooks endpoint inherits @PreAuthorize("@access.isManager()"), which only checks that the current user has manager/admin role. Any manager in any tenant can list their own tenant-scoped hooks, but can they cross tenant? Service always scopes by user tenant, so no cross-tenant object access. However manager in tenant can alter any webhook within tenant irrespective ownerId; intended manager capability likely. No finding.

findings.title: Webhook removal is racy across tenants
findings.description: Tenant filtering occurs before a separate unconditional map removal. A concurrent save can replace the same id with an entity from another tenant between findByTenantAndId and store.remove, causing deletion of the other tenant's webhook. Trigger requires concurrent operations and a colliding/reused id (the repository accepts arbitrary entity IDs through save).

findings.title: Currency conversion accepts zero rates and throws arithmetic exception
findings.description: A manager can create or update a currency with rateMicros=0 because CurrencyMapper passes the request value through without validation. An authenticated tenant caller invoking GET /api/currencies/convert with that currency as `to` reaches integer division by zero in CurrencyService.convert, producing an unhandled ArithmeticException/HTTP 500. The failure is per-request, not a process-wide outage.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint bypasses invoice tenant authorization

findings.title: Task history endpoint leaks cross-tenant activity

That service queries by entity and entityId only, so guessing a foreign task ID returns its activity, including sensitive detail.

findings.title: Task move permits cross-organisation reassignment

findings.title: Admin role enforcement trusts any authenticated admin and role changes are unrestricted
findings.description: The admin endpoints are gated by securityRules based only on the authenticated user's role, but no endpoint checks that the caller is an authorized platform administrator. Any account whose role is admin can list all users/orgs/audit records and PUT /api/admin/users/:id/role to assign arbitrary roles. Because setRole accepts req.body.role without validating it and updates any user by ID, a compromised or improperly elevated admin can promote an arbitrary user. Trigger: authenticated bearer token for an admin calls PUT /api/admin/users/{id}/role with {"role":"admin"}.

findings.title: Attachment upload filename permits path traversal writes
findings.description: An authenticated user with access to any task can submit an attachment filename containing path separators and `..`. `cleanName` only removes markup characters and trims/caps length; it does not enforce a basename. `upload` interpolates that value into the storage key after org/task IDs, and `storage.put` joins the key to `env.uploadRoot` and writes it without containment validation. A filename such as `../../../../outside` can therefore escape the upload root (depth depends on configured root and target path) and overwrite/create files writable by the service account. This is code-level evidence; no filesystem write was executed.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-controlled organization header
findings.description: Authenticated users with manager/admin role can select another tenant for billing plan and invoice data by setting X-Org-Id. billingRouter is mounted before resolveOrg, and its orgOf helper directly returns the header without checking membership; securityRules only checks the global role. GET /api/billing/invoices (or /plan) with a victim X-Org-Id exposes that organization's billing data. Static source finding; no runtime request executed.

findings.title: Hardcoded default service token exposes internal routes
findings.description: The /api/internal mount applies requireServiceToken to all internal endpoints, but env.serviceToken defaults to the literal `svc-dev-token`. Unless deployments override SERVICE_TOKEN, any remote caller who knows this source default can access internal invoice reads, full project exports, and Slack comment creation. The internal invoice route returns the full invoice object, including internalNote; the export route returns project task notes.

findings.title: Internal invoice endpoint exposes cross-organization invoice data
findings.description: Any caller with the internal service token can request an invoice by ID. Unlike invoiceService.get(user,id), getById does not scope by organization and returns the complete Invoice object, including internalNote. Seed data includes another organization's invoice with the note "ours"; other invoices may contain sensitive internal notes. This is a service-token-authorized cross-tenant data exposure.

findings.title: Internal invoice endpoint returns invoices without tenant authorization
findings.description: The service-token-protected internal invoice lookup fetches any invoice by caller-supplied ID and returns it without checking the calling service's organization scope. Any holder of the shared service token who can identify an invoice ID can read its full record, including invoice line details. The internal route has no org parameter or ownership check.

findings.title: Internal project export bypasses project authorization and returns private task notes
findings.description: The token-protected /api/internal/exports/:projectId route calls exportService.exportProject directly. That service fetches a project by ID with no organization/owner authorization and returns task notes and visibility for every top-level task. The normal project export flow calls projectService.exportFor(user,id), which requires the user's project access first. A service-token holder can therefore read exports across organizations by project ID.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint bypasses tenant ownership checks
findings.description: An authenticated caller can request GET /api/invoices/:id/pdf with another organization's invoice ID. Unlike the neighboring invoice routes, this handler calls pdfService.render directly without invoiceService.get(user, id). pdfService retrieves the invoice by ID alone and returns its body, including internalNote, so cross-tenant invoice details and internal notes are disclosed. The route is behind global authenticate and resolveOrg, but neither is an invoice ownership check.

findings.title: Public board export exposes private project tasks
findings.description: The unauthenticated GET /public/boards/:slug/export route checks only that the board is published, then passes its projectId to exportProject. That export returns every task's notes and visibility without filtering private tasks. For published board slug acme-roadmap, the route exposes the seeded private task 'Acquisition talks' and its confidential notes. Public normal board view filters visibility, but export does not.

findings.title: Search exposes comments across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated user can request GET /api/search?q=<term>; searchService scopes tasks and projects to user.orgId but calls commentRepo.search(q) without organization or task-visibility filtering. Matching comments from every organization are returned with body text (up to 160 chars), taskId, and id. Authentication and resolveOrg do not restrict this comment query.

findings.title: Search returns comments from every organization
findings.description: Any authenticated caller searching for a matching term receives comments across all tenants. Unlike tasks and projects, commentRepo.search receives no orgId, and comment records include body and taskId. A user can enumerate another organization's comment content by searching distinctive terms.

findings.title: Task history endpoint exposes activity without task authorization
findings.description: Authenticated callers can GET /api/tasks/:id/history; unlike adjacent task subresource routes, this handler does not call taskService.require(user, id) or otherwise verify that the task belongs to the caller's organization. It passes the attacker-supplied task ID directly to activityService.forEntity, which returns matching activity entries. A caller who knows or guesses another organization's task ID can retrieve its history.

findings.title: Task move permits moving tasks into another organization
findings.description: An authenticated task owner can POST /api/tasks/:id/move with another organization's projectId. taskService.move checks task access via requireWritable, but validates the target only for existence and then rewrites both projectId and orgId to the target's values. This moves the caller's task across tenant boundaries and changes ownership context. Static source finding; no runtime request executed.

findings.title: Webhook delivery endpoint exposes stored authorization tokens
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can request GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. The service verifies the webhook belongs to that user's organization, then returns every complete delivery record. Stored delivery records include requestHeaders with the outbound Authorization bearer token (confirmed by seed delivery records), disclosing webhook credentials to ordinary members.

findings.title: Attachment downloads lack task-level authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can download any attachment in that organization by knowing its id. download() only compares attachment.orgId with user.orgId; it does not invoke taskService.require or check task visibility/ownership. This permits cross-task access within a tenant.

findings.title: Comment creation permits author impersonation
findings.description: The authenticated POST /:id/comments handler sets `authorId` to the caller, then spreads `req.body` afterward. A caller-supplied `authorId` therefore overwrites the authenticated identity. Task ID and organization are explicitly reassigned afterward, but authorId is not. The comment service persists the resulting object and comment listing resolves authorName from that ID, allowing a user able to comment on a task to create comments attributed to another account. No runtime request was executed.

findings.title: Cross-owner notification disclosure within an organization
findings.description: Authenticated organization members can retrieve any notification in their organization by ID, regardless of owner. Mutation handlers enforce owner/role checks but GET /:id does not. This exposes notification titles/channels across users.

findings.title: Goal read endpoints expose organization-wide records to members
findings.description: Any authenticated member can list every goal in their organization or fetch an individual goal by ID. Unlike create, update, delete, and archive, these service methods do not call requireManager; listForOrg filters only by orgId and getInOrg verifies only org membership. This exposes manager-created goal names and targets to all members.

findings.title: Organization members can read other members’ notes
findings.description: Any authenticated member in an organization can list every note in that organization, and require() only checks orgId, so GET /api/notes/:id also returns another member's note. The model records ownerId and writes enforce ownership for members, but these read paths do not. A member can enumerate and read other members’ note titles and bodies.

findings.title: Passcodes use unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
findings.description: Registration and login use hashPasscode, which computes a single unsalted SHA-256 digest. If user records are exposed, passcodes can be tested offline at high speed and identical passcodes have identical hashes. Use a password hashing function designed to resist offline guessing, with per-user salts and tunable cost.

findings.title: Private task data exposed to organization peers
findings.description: The task endpoints check only organization membership when reading tasks, but do not enforce task.visibility or ownership. Any authenticated user in the same org can retrieve another user's private task via GET /:id, and GET /?projectId=... lists private and public tasks alike. The task model explicitly distinguishes private/public, and create defaults visibility to private.

findings.title: Public invoice share tokens remain valid after their expiry timestamp
findings.description: readShareToken parses and returns expiresAt but does not reject expired claims. The public invoice route checks expiry itself, but any other consumer of readShareToken may accept expired tokens. Within this batch, verify consumers; if the helper is only used by the public invoice route this specific concern is not exploitable.

findings.title: Service-token Slack integration permits forged comments as any same-organization user
findings.description: The internal Slack comments route accepts taskId and authorEmail from the caller and only checks that the selected author belongs to the task's organization. Any holder of the shared service token can create a comment on any task while attributing it to any user in that organization; there is no proof that the caller is Slack or that the author actually submitted the comment. This enables impersonation and untrusted comment insertion.

findings.title: Timesheet read exposes other users' records within an organization
findings.description: Any authenticated organization member can GET /api/timesheets/:id for any timesheet in their org. The param handler confirms only orgId, then GET returns the entire row without checking owner; write paths do check ownership for members. This exposes other members' hours/week data.

findings.title: Default token signing secret permits forged authentication tokens
findings.description: When TOKEN_SECRET is unset, the application signs and verifies bearer tokens with the public literal `workspace-dev-secret`. An unauthenticated caller who knows this value can compute a valid HMAC token for a chosen user ID; authenticate() accepts it when that user exists, granting that account's privileges. This affects the login-protected automation and attachment routes as well as the rest of the API. Exploitability depends on deployment leaving TOKEN_SECRET unset.

findings.title: Billing routes trust unvalidated X-Org-Id
findings.description: The billing router is mounted before resolveOrg in createApp, so requests handled by /api/billing never pass the membership check. billing.ts orgOf directly uses X-Org-Id when present, and /plan and /invoices query that organization. Any authenticated manager (allowed by securityRules for /api/billing) can supply another tenant's ID and read its plan/payment-method last four digits and invoice metadata.

findings.title: Cross-organization comment search leaks comment contents
findings.description: commentRepo.search filters only by body text and has no organization constraint. searchService invokes it for any authenticated user's query and returns comment body snippets and task IDs without checking the comment's org/task visibility. A user in one organization can search for a distinctive phrase from another organization's comments and receive matching contents and identifiers.

findings.title: Default token secret permits forged public invoice share tokens
findings.description: When TOKEN_SECRET is unset, tokens.ts signs share claims with the publicly known fallback `workspace-dev-secret` (config/env.ts:2; tokens.ts:4-5,31-39). The unauthenticated GET /public/invoices/:token handler accepts any correctly signed, unexpired claim whose kind is `invoice`, then calls publicView(claim.id) (routes/public.ts:12-15). An attacker can construct a share token for a known invoice ID and retrieve its customer, amount, status, and line items without authorization. The route has no additional ownership check; the signed token is its access control.

findings.title: Internal project export lacks project authorization
findings.description: GET /api/internal/exports/:projectId passes the caller-supplied projectId directly to exportService.exportProject. That service uses projectRepo.get(projectId) without checking organization or caller access, then returns the project's name and task titles, notes, statuses, and visibility. The route is behind requireServiceToken, but that authenticates possession of one shared service token, not authorization for a particular project. Any holder of that token can enumerate known project IDs and retrieve project data across organizations.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint exposes invoices across organisations
findings.description: Any authenticated user who can obtain or guess an invoice id can retrieve its rendered details regardless of tenant. The ordinary invoice get path calls invoiceService.get(user,id), which checks orgId, but the PDF route bypasses that check and pdfService.render includes internalNote.

findings.title: Invoice PDF endpoint skips tenant ownership check
findings.description: Any authenticated user can request GET /api/invoices/:id/pdf with another organization's invoice ID. Unlike the other invoice routes, this handler passes the ID directly to pdfService.render; render reads the invoice by ID without checking its orgId against the caller. The response includes customer, line items, amounts, and internalNote, so this is cross-tenant invoice data disclosure.

findings.title: Manager can read another organisation's billing data via X-Org-Id
findings.description: The billing router derives its target organisation from a caller-controlled X-Org-Id header before the organisation-membership resolver runs. securityRules only requires manager/admin role, so an authenticated manager can request another organisation's billing plan or invoice list by supplying its id.

findings.title: Published board export exposes non-public project tasks
findings.description: The unauthenticated /public/boards/:slug/export route only checks that the board is published, then calls exportProject for the entire project. Unlike publicView, exportProject returns every task including non-public tasks and notes. A published board slug therefore permits disclosure of project data not marked public.

findings.title: Search returns comments from every organization
findings.description: Any authenticated user who searches for a substring receives matching comments from all organizations. Task and project search are scoped to user.orgId, but commentRepo.search accepts only the query and scans all comments; results include comment body and taskId. This leaks cross-tenant content and identifiers via GET /api/search?q=...

findings.title: Task attachment filename permits path traversal in upload storage key
findings.description: An authenticated same-organization user can submit a filename containing path separators and dot segments. `cleanName` removes markup characters and truncates but does not remove `/`, `\`, or leading dots (src/lib/sanitize.ts:6-8). The upload constructs a storage key directly from the task's org/id and this name (src/services/attachmentService.ts:17-20); `storage.put` joins that key to `uploadRoot` and writes it without containment validation (src/lib/storage.ts:6-10). Traversal segments can escape the intended task directory and, if enough `../` segments are supplied, the upload root, allowing overwrite/create of files writable by the service account. Route requires authentication via app middleware; taskService.require only limits to the user's organization, not task ownership.

findings.title: Task history endpoint exposes activity without task authorization
findings.description: GET /api/tasks/:id/history passes the caller-supplied task ID directly to activityService.forEntity without first calling taskService.require. That service queries activity entries by entity and entityId only and applies no organization/ownership check. Any authenticated user who knows or guesses another tenant's task ID can retrieve its activity history.

findings.title: Task move can transfer tasks across organizations
findings.description: An authenticated member who owns a task can call POST /api/tasks/:id/move with any existing projectId. The service checks write access to the source task, but looks up the destination project globally and never verifies target.orgId === user.orgId. It then updates both projectId and orgId to the target values, transferring the task (including notes, watchers and other task data) into another organization.

findings.title: Comment creation permits authorId spoofing
findings.description: An authenticated caller with access to a task can POST a comment with another user's authorId. The route places user.id before the untrusted request body in the object passed to commentService.add, so req.body.authorId overwrites the authenticated identity; commentService persists the supplied authorId. Subsequent comment listing resolves authorName from that ID, enabling forged attribution.

findings.title: Dashboard handlers ignore resolved organization context for admins
findings.description: Dashboard listing and creation scope exclusively to user.orgId, while resolveOrg explicitly permits an admin to select another organization via X-Org-Id and stores that selection as req.org. Dashboard routes pass only req.user, so the selected organization is ignored. This causes cross-org admin requests to list/create in the admin's home organization rather than the requested one; it does not allow non-admin cross-tenant access. Confirmed design/context mismatch, with integrity/availability implications limited to unexpected organization placement for admin operations.

findings.title: Members can alter approval state of their own requests
findings.description: Any authenticated member can create approval records and can update their own approval, including setting its state to an arbitrary value. The route's ownership guard permits writes by the owner; neither validator nor service restricts state transitions or requires an approver role. This allows self-approval if consumers treat state as authoritative.

findings.title: Members can read other members’ API key records and notifications
findings.description: The authenticated API exposes organization-wide records at GET /api/api-keys and GET /api/notifications. apiKeyService.list and notificationService.list filter only by orgId, and callers receive full model rows including ownerId and, for API keys, their scope. Individual notification GET also checks only that the record belongs to the active org; API-key GET likewise uses org rather than owner. This leaks cross-user metadata to any member in the org. No key secret is present in the ApiKey model, so the evidenced impact is metadata disclosure, not credential recovery.

findings.title: Poll writes allow managers to modify or delete any organization poll
findings.description: PUT /api/polls/:id and DELETE /api/polls/:id call requireWritable. That helper rejects only when the caller is a member and is not the owner, so manager callers can change or delete any poll in their organization. This bypasses the apparent owner restriction for non-admin elevated users. Authentication and resolveOrg constrain access to authenticated users/org context; no route role middleware restricts these handlers.

findings.title: Project task listing and export disclose private task notes to org peers
findings.description: An authenticated user in the same organization can read every task attached to a project, including tasks marked visibility="private" and their notes, without being the owner or watcher. GET /:id/tasks calls listForProject after only checking project organization; GET /:id/export similarly serializes all project tasks and notes. Trigger: create or identify a private task in a same-org project, then request either endpoint as another org user. This conflicts with the explicit private visibility field and exposes task content across users.

findings.title: Reminder item authorization permits all non-member roles
findings.description: The canWrite predicate authorizes any caller whose role is not exactly "member" to update or delete every reminder in their organization. The ID parameter loader constrains the reminder to the active organization, but does not constrain its owner. Thus a non-owner user with any other role (for example a viewer) can PUT or DELETE another user's reminder by ID. Restrict writes to the owner and explicitly authorized manager/admin roles.

findings.title: Webhook delivery endpoint exposes stored authorization headers
findings.description: Any authenticated user in an organization can call GET /api/webhooks/:id/deliveries. The service checks only that the webhook belongs to the caller's organization, then returns complete delivery records, including requestHeaders. Those headers contain Authorization bearer credentials in the seeded delivery examples, exposing webhook auth tokens to ordinary members; the write endpoints' manager-only gate is mounted after this route and does not protect it.

findings.title: Comment creation permits author impersonation
findings.description: The task comment route sets authorId from the authenticated user, then spreads the request body afterward, allowing a caller to overwrite authorId. commentService.add persists that object, and commentService.list resolves authorName from the stored authorId. A caller with access to a task can create comments attributed to another user, corrupting audit/accountability records.

findings.title: Members can enumerate organization-wide integration link records
findings.description: Any authenticated organization member can list integration links belonging to other users. GET /api/integration-links passes the current user to integrationLinkService.list, which returns all rows for user.orgId without an ownership or role filter. Responses include ownerId, provider, and externalId. The per-record GET also requires only same-org membership. Writes are restricted to managers, but read access is not.

findings.title: Check cross-tenant IDOR in tag endpoints
findings.description: Tag read, update, delete and archive operations are constrained to the authenticated user's org. The service passes user.orgId to repository methods, and the repository verifies row.orgId before returning, updating, or removing. Create binds orgId and ownerId from authenticated user. No vulnerability found in scoped routes.

findings.title: Billing endpoints disclose cross-tenant subscription and invoice data
findings.description: Authenticated callers can select an arbitrary tenant with X-Tenant-Id on billing endpoints. TenantFilter explicitly skips /api/billing, SecurityConfig requires only authentication, and BillingController forwards the supplied tenant ID directly to BillingService, which reads subscription and invoices without an ownership check.

findings.title: Export name permits path traversal outside export directory
findings.description: ExportService uses Text.plain on a user-supplied name and resolves that value plus .csv against exportDir. Text.plain removes markup and whitespace but retains slash and dot-dot segments. A name such as ../outside can cause Files.writeString to write outside the configured export directory, subject to process filesystem permissions.

findings.title: Global search returns comments across tenant boundaries
findings.description: GlobalSearchService correctly scopes expense and vendor results but appends results from comments.search(q) without tenant or expense authorization filtering. CommentRepository searches every stored comment body, so any authenticated user can obtain matching comment contents and IDs from other tenants.

findings.title: Nested admin mutations are accessible to ordinary tenant users
findings.description: The security matcher protects only /api/admin/*, while role changes, deactivation, and tenant limit updates are deeper paths. They fall through to authenticated() authorization. AdminService only checks target tenant membership and permits the caller to assign any role, including ADMIN, deactivate users, or change limits.

findings.title: Public statement token is not bound to requested statement
findings.description: The public statement handler verifies that the supplied token has some subject, discards that subject, and builds the statement identified by the caller-controlled path parameter. A valid token for one statement therefore authorizes retrieval of another known statement ID.

findings.title: Receipt download endpoint allows cross-tenant receipt access
findings.description: The receipt download route accepts only a receipt ID, does not receive the authenticated user, and calls a globally scoped repository lookup. Unlike neighboring receipt operations, it never authorizes access through the associated expense. Any authenticated user who knows a receipt ID can retrieve its bytes.

findings.title: Service integration can write comments with caller-supplied tenant and expense IDs
findings.description: The integration comments endpoint is restricted to SERVICE role, but accepts tenantId, expenseId and authorId from request body and CommentService.add persists them directly without verifying the expense belongs to that tenant or that the author is valid. Any compromised/overprivileged SERVICE credential can attribute arbitrary comments to arbitrary identities/expenses; downstream listing is keyed only by expenseId.

findings.title: Admin nested routes bypass administrator role matcher
findings.description: SecurityConfig restricts only /api/admin/* to ROLE_ADMIN. That Ant-style pattern matches one path segment after /api/admin, so nested mutation routes such as /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and /api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits do not match it and fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). AdminUserController exposes role changes and deactivation; AdminService checks same-tenant membership but does not require an admin role. A normal authenticated tenant user can promote themself (or another same-tenant user) to ADMIN, then access admin operations.

findings.title: Billing endpoints trust caller-supplied tenant ID
findings.description: Authenticated callers can select an arbitrary tenant by setting X-Tenant-Id on /api/billing/plan or /api/billing/invoices. BillingController passes this header directly to BillingService, which retrieves subscription/invoices for that tenant. TenantFilter explicitly skips /api/billing, so its authenticated-user tenant binding and mismatch rejection never apply. This permits cross-tenant billing data disclosure to any authenticated user who knows or guesses a tenant ID.

findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver identity
findings.description: Bulk approval uses request.approverId as the deciding identity instead of the authenticated actor. The self-approval guard compares requesterId against this client-controlled value, and the same value is persisted as decidedBy and audit actor. A manager can supply any other ID to approve their own request and forge attribution.

findings.title: Export name allows writing files outside export directory
findings.description: An authenticated user can submit an export name containing path traversal, such as ../../some-file, because Text.plain removes markup and whitespace only. ExportService resolves that name directly beneath exportDir and writes the generated CSV, so the path can escape the configured export directory and overwrite files writable by the service account.

findings.title: Global search leaks comments across tenants
findings.description: Any authenticated user can search comments globally. GlobalSearchService scopes expenses and vendors to the authenticated tenant, but comments.search(q) has no tenant, expense ownership, or visibility filter and returns every matching comment body from the in-memory repository. Searching a distinctive phrase can disclose other tenants' comments.

findings.title: Project expense transfer accepts cross-tenant target project
findings.description: An authenticated project manager can POST /api/projects/{sourceId}/transfer-expenses with a targetProjectId belonging to another tenant. The service checks source ownership/tenant but loads target by unscoped findById and reassigns all source expenses to that foreign project ID. This changes associations across tenant boundaries and can expose the expenses through the target tenant's project endpoint.

findings.title: Receipt download bypasses expense ownership and tenant authorization
findings.description: The authenticated receipt download endpoint loads a receipt directly by receiptId and returns its content without checking the caller's tenant, ownership, or access to the associated expense. Knowing or obtaining another receipt ID is sufficient to retrieve its bytes.

findings.title: Share token for one statement authorizes any statement
findings.description: The public statement endpoint verifies only that a signed token has the stmt: prefix, discards its subject, and then loads the statement selected by the caller-controlled path id. A token issued for one account therefore grants unauthenticated access to any known statement id.

findings.title: Vendor bank-detail writes lack tenant authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated user can call PUT /api/tenants/{tenantId}/vendors/{id}/bank-details without the @PreAuthorize tenant-management check used by adjacent vendor routes. The service scopes lookup only to caller-supplied tenantId, not authenticated user's tenant; TenantFilter only constrains X-Tenant-Id, not this path parameter. A user can overwrite another tenant's vendor bank account details, enabling payment redirection.

findings.title: Expense comment endpoint accepts forged author identity
findings.description: Authenticated users with access to an expense can submit comments with an arbitrary authorId. The controller overwrites tenantId and expenseId but preserves authorId from the request; CommentService persists it unchanged, enabling comment impersonation and misleading attribution.

findings.title: Billing endpoints allow cross-tenant invoice and subscription reads
findings.description: Any authenticated caller can supply another tenant's X-Tenant-Id to GET /api/billing/plan or /api/billing/invoices. SecurityConfig only requires authentication for these paths, and TenantFilter explicitly exempts /api/billing, so no tenant binding is performed. BillingService uses the caller-supplied tenant ID directly to retrieve subscription and invoices. This exposes another tenant's plan/seats/renewal date and invoice numbers, amounts, statuses, and issue dates.

findings.title: Billing tenant header permits cross-tenant subscription and invoice reads
findings.description: TenantFilter explicitly skips all /api/billing requests. BillingController then accepts X-Tenant-Id directly and passes it to BillingService, whose repository looks up subscriptions and invoices for that tenant without comparing it to the authenticated principal. Any authenticated caller who can guess or obtain another tenant ID can read its plan and invoices.

findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver identity
findings.description: An authenticated MANAGER or ADMIN can POST /api/approvals/bulk-approve with another user's approverId and an approval ID in their tenant. The controller role gate does not bind that field to the authenticated principal; approveAll passes request.approverId() to decide(), which only rejects when it equals the requesterId. The forged identity is saved as decidedBy and written into the audit entry, enabling impersonated approval/rejection attribution and bypassing the intended self-approval constraint when approverId is set to the actual actor's requester identity. Require decisions to be attributed to actor.id() and use that identity for the self-approval check.

findings.title: Cross-tenant project transfer exposes expenses
findings.description: A manager who can manage a source project can provide any existing targetProjectId. The code loads the target globally with findById but never checks target.tenantId against the caller/source tenant, then reassigns all source expenses to that project. A user in the target tenant can subsequently retrieve those expenses through expensesOf(target), which checks the project's tenant but queries expenses solely by project ID.

findings.title: Export name permits path traversal and overwrites arbitrary files
findings.description: An authenticated caller of POST /api/exports controls ExportRequest.name. Text.plain sanitizes presentation characters, but the value is concatenated into exportDir.resolve(name + ".csv") without enforcing a single filename segment or checking the normalized path remains under exportDir. A name containing ../ can therefore write the rendered tenant expense CSV outside the export directory, overwriting any file writable by the service account. Manager/owner filtering restricts rows but does not constrain the filesystem target.

findings.title: Global search exposes comments across tenants and owners
findings.description: Authenticated callers to /api/search receive matching comments from the repository without tenant or ownership filtering. GlobalSearchService filters expenses by tenant and owner/manager and limits vendors to managers, but returns every result of CommentRepository.search, including each comment body, regardless of the authenticated user's tenant or access to its expense.

findings.title: Integration comment relay trusts caller-supplied identity and tenant
findings.description: Any authenticated SERVICE-role caller can POST /api/integrations/comments with arbitrary tenantId, expenseId, and authorId. IntegrationCommentController passes the body directly to CommentService.add, which persists those fields without checking that the expense exists, belongs to the tenant, or that the author belongs to the tenant. This permits forged comments associated with another tenant/expense and arbitrary attribution; callers may also create dangling records.

findings.title: Integration comment relay trusts caller-supplied tenant and expense IDs
findings.description: Any caller authenticated with the SERVICE role can submit CommentInput directly to CommentService.add. Unlike the user comment route, this path does not resolve the expense or derive tenant/author from a scoped principal; add persists input.tenantId, input.expenseId and input.authorId verbatim. A compromised or over-privileged integration credential can inject comments into arbitrary tenants/expenses and impersonate authors. This appears intentional relay functionality but lacks resource-level validation.

findings.title: Nested admin routes bypass the ADMIN role matcher
findings.description: SecurityConfig restricts only `/api/admin/*` to ADMIN, but the admin controllers are nested paths such as `/api/admin/users/{id}/roles` and `/api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits`. The single-segment pattern does not match these deeper paths, so they fall through to `.anyRequest().authenticated()`. AdminService.changeRole and updateLimits enforce tenant equality but no administrator role; any authenticated tenant user can change another user's role (including promoting to ADMIN) or alter tenant limits. The same exposure applies to deactivate. This is source-verified; runtime matcher behavior was not exercised.

findings.title: Share token is not bound to requested statement
findings.description: The public statement endpoint validates that the supplied token is a valid statement-share token, but discards its subject and then builds the statement named by the independent path id. Anyone holding a valid link for statement A can replace the path id with another statement B and receive B's full statement view.

findings.title: Tenant admin can grant SERVICE role and access service-only APIs
findings.description: An authenticated ADMIN can submit a RoleChange with role SERVICE for any user in the same tenant. changeRole persists that role without restricting assignable roles. BearerAuthFilter subsequently creates ROLE_SERVICE authority from the stored user role, and SecurityConfig grants /api/integrations/** and /internal/** to that authority. TenantFilter also skips tenant context enforcement for SERVICE principals. A tenant administrator can therefore convert a controlled account into a service principal and reach service-only operations; downstream endpoint controls determine the ultimate cross-tenant impact.

findings.title: Unauthenticated receipt download exposes receipt contents
findings.description: The receipt download route accepts only a receiptId and calls ReceiptService.load directly; it supplies no authenticated principal and performs no tenant, expense ownership, or caller authorization check. SecurityConfig requires authentication on routes outside /public/**, so an attacker with any authenticated account can request a known receipt ID and receive its raw content. Receipt IDs generated by Ids.next are not shown to be secret authorization tokens. Other receipt routes enforce ownership through ExpenseService.get, but this route bypasses those checks.

findings.title: CSV export does not neutralize spreadsheet formulas
findings.description: An authenticated user can create an expense whose description begins with a spreadsheet formula marker (for example `=HYPERLINK(...)`). Export rendering encloses the description in quotes but does not neutralize formula-leading values; CSV quoting is not formula escaping. When an exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software, the field may execute as a formula. Expense descriptions are included in exports at these lines.

findings.title: Currency conversion permits divide-by-zero rates and overflowing arithmetic
findings.description: A manager can create or update a tenant currency with rateMicros zero or an extreme value; CurrencyMapper stores dto.rateMicros() without validation. Any authenticated tenant user can call GET /api/currencies/convert with chosen amount. A zero target rate throws ArithmeticException; multiplication can overflow signed long before division and return a materially incorrect amount. This can disrupt conversions or corrupt downstream financial decisions.

findings.title: Notes allow cross-owner linking to another user's expense
findings.description: An authenticated user who can create or edit their own note can set linkedExpenseId to any expense ID owned by another user in the same tenant if ExpenseService.get permits manager-wide access only? NoteService.validate calls expenses.get(user, id), which enforces ExpenseService access policy; inspect reveals validation accordingly. No finding: validation enforces caller's expense visibility. (discard)

findings.title: Per-diem records expose financial fields to every tenant member
findings.description: Any authenticated user in a tenant can list every member's per-diem records, including destination, days, and rateCents. The controller explicitly allows tenant-wide reads, and list filters only by tenant, not owner or a narrower authorized role. Trigger: call GET /api/per-diems as any tenant member. This is a tenant-scoped confidentiality exposure.

findings.title: Policy list exposes all tenant policies to any manager
findings.description: Any authenticated manager passes the controller-wide @PreAuthorize check, and list() returns every policy for that manager's tenant. Unlike the entity's ownerId, no owner-or-manager policy is needed to constrain results. If policies are intended to be owner-scoped, a manager can enumerate other users' policy names/rules/limits. Manager role and same-tenant membership are prerequisites; confirm whether tenant-wide manager access is intended.

findings.title: Purchase order input controls workflow status
findings.description: Purchase-order create and update copy dto.status directly into persisted records. Any authenticated owner can create or update an order with statuses such as RECEIVED or arbitrary values, bypassing the receive endpoint's OPEN-only transition and its intended state transition. No status validation/control appears in PurchaseOrderService.validate.

findings.title: Tag attachment bypasses expense ownership authorization
findings.description: A caller who owns or manages a tag can attach it to any expense in the same tenant, including another user's expense. TagController checks permission only against the tag owner; TagService.attach calls expenses.get(user, expenseId), which checks that the caller owns the expense or is a manager, so actually this is prevented. No issue here.

findings.title: Template publish path can escape tenant directory
findings.description: A manager/admin can create or update a template with a name consisting of dots. Text.safeSegment strips leading dots until empty, returning "unnamed", so that example itself is contained; however its filtering limits separators and dot sequences. Tenant directory component is AuthUser.tenantId derived from authenticated user, not request input. No traversal is apparent for template names. This is not a confirmed issue.

findings.title: Public status endpoint discloses service version
findings.description: Unauthenticated GET /status returns the fixed service name and exact version 1.14.2. SecurityConfig explicitly permits /status to all callers. This exposes deployment/version fingerprinting information, which can assist targeting version-specific weaknesses; no sensitive data or direct exploit is shown.

findings.title: Asset routes enforce tenant and ownership controls
findings.description: Review of all five AssetController routes found controls in service/mapper and controller: list is tenant scoped, id lookup rejects other-tenant rows, create derives tenant and owner from AuthUser, and mutations enforce owner-or-manager while preserving current tenant/owner.

findings.title: Audit entry routes require manager and tenant scope
findings.description: Both audit-entry read routes are guarded by class-level manager authorization. Their service also scopes list and item retrieval to the authenticated user's tenant; cross-tenant IDs resolve as not found.

findings.title: Webhook routes: no confirmed vulnerability
findings.description: No vulnerabilities should be recorded as findings. This tool is only for vulnerabilities; route verdicts will be reported to parent.
