findings.title: Bulk approval trusts caller-supplied approver identity
findings.description: The manager/admin-only bulk approval endpoint accepts approverId in the request body and uses it as the deciding identity. The self-approval check compares requesterId against this caller-controlled value rather than the authenticated actor. A manager can therefore approve their own pending expense by supplying any different approverId, bypassing the segregation-of-duties rule; the forged identity is also persisted in the approval and audit entry.

findings.title: Cross-tenant expense transfer via project target ID
findings.description: An authenticated project manager can POST /api/projects/{sourceId}/transfer-expenses with targetProjectId set to any project ID. The source is verified as managed and tenant-scoped, but target is only loaded by ID; its tenant is never compared. ExpenseRepository.reassign moves every source expense to that foreign project ID. A user in the target tenant can then retrieve those source-tenant expenses through GET /api/projects/{targetId}/expenses, which queries solely by project ID.

findings.title: Export name permits path traversal during CSV write
findings.description: An authenticated caller can POST /api/exports with a name containing path separators and parent-directory components. ExportService applies Text.plain, which strips markup/normalizes whitespace but does not constrain path components, then resolves name + ".csv" against exportDir and writes it. A name such as ../../outside writes outside the configured export directory (subject to process filesystem permissions), allowing overwrite/create of files reachable by the service account. Export reads remain tenant/owner-or-manager checked; this finding concerns creation-time filesystem write.

findings.title: Global search discloses comments across tenants and ownership boundaries
findings.description: An authenticated caller can issue GET /api/search?q=<3+ chars>. Expense matches are tenant-scoped and filtered to the owner unless manager, and vendor search is manager-only, but comment matches are appended without tenant or expense-ownership filtering. CommentRepository.search scans all stored comments by body. This exposes comment bodies (and IDs) from other tenants or expenses to any authenticated user whose search query matches.

findings.title: Nested admin routes bypass the ADMIN role matcher
findings.description: SecurityConfig restricts only /api/admin/* to ROLE_ADMIN. The admin mutation endpoints are nested paths such as PUT /api/admin/users/{id}/roles and POST /api/admin/users/{id}/deactivate, which do not match the single-level wildcard. They therefore fall through to anyRequest().authenticated(). AdminService.changeRole/deactivate enforce tenant equality but do not enforce an admin role, so any authenticated user in the target user's tenant can change roles (including grant ADMIN) or deactivate users.

findings.title: Public statement endpoint ignores the share token's bound statement ID
findings.description: PublicStatementController validates that the supplied token is a share token but discards its subject, then serves the statement selected by the independent path id. A holder of any valid share token can substitute another statement ID (if known or enumerable) and retrieve that statement without owner/tenant authorization. ShareTokenService embeds the statement ID in the signed subject, so the endpoint can and should require it to equal the requested id.

findings.title: Receipt download lacks tenant and expense authorization
findings.description: Any authenticated caller can download a receipt by its receiptId without supplying or validating an authorized expense. ReceiptController.download invokes ReceiptService.load directly; load performs only a repository lookup and does not check tenant, expense ownership, or caller identity. Receipt IDs are generated from a process-wide incrementing sequence (Ids.next), making enumeration feasible. A caller can therefore retrieve receipt contents belonging to other tenants if they discover/guess IDs.

findings.title: Template publishing permits tenant path traversal
findings.description: A manager/admin can publish a tenant template. The output directory is built by resolving the authenticated user's tenantId directly beneath the configured template directory, without normalizing or constraining the result. If tenantId contains path separators or traversal components (e.g. ../../outside), dir and target escape templatePath; publishing then writes attacker-controlled template body to that filesystem location. Authenticated role requirement applies to writes, but does not prevent a manager in a tenant with a crafted tenant identifier from escaping the intended directory.

findings.title: Budget updates let owners forge spent and limit amounts
findings.description: An authenticated owner can PUT /api/budgets/{id} with arbitrary limitCents and spentCents. BudgetMapper.apply copies both client-supplied monetary fields directly into the stored Budget, and remaining() reports limitCents - spentCents. This lets a user falsify budget utilization (including making remaining negative or inflating it), affecting financial reporting for their budget. Tenant and owner checks are present; the flaw is writable accounting state, not cross-tenant access.

findings.title: Currency conversion overflows on attacker-controlled amount
findings.description: The GET /api/currencies/convert handler accepts an arbitrary signed 64-bit amount, and CurrencyService.convert multiplies it by the source rate before dividing. That multiplication uses Java long arithmetic and silently wraps on overflow, producing an incorrect conversion result (including negative amounts) rather than rejecting or safely computing the result. Any authenticated tenant user can trigger this calculation; impact is incorrect financial amount output, not direct mutation of stored records.

findings.title: Expense submission lets managers submit another owner's draft
findings.description: The shared get() authorization admits either the expense owner or any manager (ExpenseService.java:35-39). submit() uses that guard, checks only that the record is a DRAFT, then transitions it to SUBMITTED and opens approval (lines 68-75). A manager in the same tenant can therefore submit another employee's draft, an action distinct from merely viewing it; the service does not enforce owner-only submission. This intentionally broad manager access may or may not match product policy, but authorization is the underlying concern.

findings.title: Integration comment relay accepts attacker-chosen author identity
findings.description: An authenticated SERVICE-role caller can submit POST /api/integrations/comments with an arbitrary authorId. IntegrationCommentController passes the request CommentInput directly to CommentService.add; add persists input.authorId without binding it to the authenticated service principal or validating the referenced user. The route’s SERVICE-role restriction prevents ordinary users from reaching this, but any service credential holder can attribute comments to another user, corrupting the audit identity shown with the comment.

findings.title: Tax calculation overflows for large amountCents
findings.description: An authenticated tenant user can supply amountCents to GET /api/tax-rates/{id}/apply. TaxRateService.apply multiplies that attacker-controlled long by percentBp before dividing by 10000, without range validation or checked arithmetic. For sufficiently large amounts, Java long overflow wraps and returns an incorrect (potentially negative) tax amount. The rate is tenant-scoped; changing it requires MANAGER/ADMIN, but any authenticated tenant user can trigger overflow against an existing positive rate.

findings.title: Tenant limits update bypasses admin role check
findings.description: The security matcher `/api/admin/*` is a single-segment wildcard, so it does not match `/api/admin/tenants/{id}/limits`. That route reaches `AdminService.updateLimits`, which checks only that the actor belongs to the tenant and then saves caller-provided limits; it never requires ADMIN/MANAGER. Any authenticated user in a tenant can raise that tenant's user and monthly-expense limits. Static source finding; route matcher behavior follows Spring path matching semantics.

findings.title: Webhook management authorization ignores tenant boundary
findings.description: The controller-wide method-security expression only checks whether the caller has a manager/admin role; unlike AccessPolicy.canManage(tenantId), it does not bind that authority to a tenant. An authenticated manager from any tenant can therefore call the webhook endpoints, including list, create, update, delete and ping. List and mutations in WebhookService are tenant-scoped, so this permits access to and management of webhooks in the caller's own tenant, but does not establish cross-tenant object access. The defect is role-only authorization relative to tenant-scoped management policy.

findings.title: Webhook URL accepts arbitrary destinations
findings.description: Authenticated tenant managers can create or update a webhook URL with any non-empty string. WebhookMapper calls Text.required, which only strips markup and checks emptiness; there is no URL scheme, host, or private-address validation. This permits storing destinations such as http://127.0.0.1/ or cloud metadata addresses. The reviewed ping method does not make outbound requests, and no delivery caller exists in this unit, so actual SSRF depends on a consumer elsewhere; the demonstrated issue is acceptance and persistence of unsafe webhook targets.
